# Zip Output Stream Call Flow

In legacy code reading, `lib/zip/output_stream.rb` was consistently placed on the output side. The phrase output stream in the filename made this path look straightforward: the caller passed in the content to be archived, and the file passed that content on to the archive output. Early searches therefore always started here, rather than at the read side or from the filesystem view.

The diagram from that time is still below. It defines a reading order, not an interface index.

```text
Caller
  |
  v
lib/zip/output_stream.rb
  |
  v
Archive output
```

The two arrows in the diagram were understood as a single continuous write path. On the caller side, the only question was who sent content to the output stream; on the output side, the only question was whether the archive result appeared. Under that framing, missing archive content, an abnormal write-out order, or an unusable result file should all first lead back to `lib/zip/output_stream.rb`. Direct dependencies found within the file were treated as the next segment of this path, not drawn as separate parallel entry points.

The diagram did not represent the objects' actual types, nor did it break out every name in the file. The practice at the time was to place all dependencies directly visible in the file after the output stream, treating them as merely continuing to pass the same archive content downstream. When a dependency was reached, the first question was whether it still served the write path; the default answer was yes, so no separate entry point or backtracking path was kept for it.

This arrangement shaped failure investigation. When the result file had been generated but its contents were wrong, the notes placed the problem somewhere after the content entered the output stream; when the result file did not appear, the output stream was still treated as the first place to look. The old diagram did not distinguish between the two cases because it retained only the delivery direction, not the state of intermediate objects.

Failure exits within the file were also folded into the same path at the time. They were not treated as branches in the call relationship, but as markers that the write-out had failed to reach its endpoint. As a result, the initial inspection did not work backward from a failure exit to infer another entry point; it only returned to the call site before the output stream. This was the troubleshooting order left at the time, not a comparison of all write scenarios.

The old notes called the output stream the "main entry point for the write process." This judgment was useful for narrowing the scope of the first code pass: read in the output direction first, then decide whether to trace back to the caller. It also imposed a strong assumption—all archive writes would converge here. There are no branches in the diagram precisely because branches were not considered entities that needed to be retained at the time.

When the review note was added later, the diagram was not changed; a reading constraint was added beside it: direct dependencies could still be followed, but the path should not immediately be drawn as multiple lines just because multiple dependencies appeared. The old record treated the extra names as still part of the output stream; only when they no longer passed content toward the archive output were they worth opening a separate investigation line. This condition was not elaborated further.

The review also added a note about reading order. First inspect the output boundary defined by the file itself, then see what the direct dependencies hand to the next layer; only when the archive result differs from expectations should you return to the upstream caller. With this reading, callers are not a list to enumerate one by one, but clues for locating the hop immediately before the output stream. Archive output is not an independent object list either; it is merely the endpoint of this old diagram.

That gives this page a very narrow scope: from the caller to `lib/zip/output_stream.rb`, then to archive output. It does not list callers or break archive output into a result checklist. When following the diagram, first confirm that the content entered this file, then check whether the direct dependencies continue in the same output direction; objects that could not be found on this page were all left for later reading at the time.

The DOC-08 pair consists of notes left by the same reading pass. The scattered judgments in them were not folded into the diagram here, to avoid mistaking marginal notes for call relationships. The existing diagram is still recorded as a linear write path: the caller hands off to the output stream, and the output stream completes the archive write.

# Compression Registration and Empty Stream Decision Record

Keep compression registry lookup and empty stream state in a single record to start with. The two have not been identified as the same implementation issue; at the time, they merely both fell near the decompression side, and both were easy to gloss over with an overly quick judgment: registration does not mean a later retrieval returned the expected object, and seeing an empty stream does not mean that stream was never established.

The initial entry point is `lib/zip/decompressor.rb`. This entry point is enough to start examining compression method registration and retrieval, but not enough to determine where stream creation, reading, or termination belongs. When an empty stream is observed, at least record whether the observation was before or after metadata handoff; without that position, it cannot be classified directly as missing input.

The decision for this round is to document the two tracks in parallel, without first combining the fixes.

- On the registration side, "the table contains the corresponding method" is not the stopping point. The subsequent lookup needs to be examined on its own.
- Do not treat an empty stream as stateless. Empty content is an observation, not a lifecycle conclusion.

The working hypothesis in the old notes was that most empty streams come from missing input, so they do not need to be reviewed alongside compression method registration. There are no counterexamples to this hypothesis yet, nor enough evidence to support it. It is not a basis for interface decisions.

To add: the relationship between the object passed in at registration and the lookup result; changes in the empty stream before and after metadata handoff; whether any single caller goes through both tracks.

# Compression Registration and Empty Stream Decision Record

This page retains the first version's approach of documenting compression registry lookup and empty stream state together. That does not mean the two terms refer to the same failure, or that `lib/zip/decompressor.rb` covers the entire reader lifecycle. They were placed together at the time because the decompression-side name provided the first lead, and the empty stream happened to have been described as an overly simple outcome.

## Scope Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial assessment was narrow: compression method registration, lookup, and the state of an empty stream could not be considered settled based on names or apparent results alone.

On the registration side, a common leap is to see a compression method and write "lookup is working." This conflates three things: the name of the compression method, the registry entry, and the result actually returned by a subsequent lookup. The first version could not determine whether objects were copied, wrapped, or cached, so it left those implementation guesses out.

On the empty stream side, the leap is to treat empty content as meaning there is no lifecycle to trace. This was convenient at the time because it allowed the issue to be handed back to the input side. But it did not say whether the observation was made before stream creation, during reading, before metadata handoff, or after handoff. Without a stage, empty is just an observation.

The original decision stands: the registration and empty stream tracks can be maintained on the same page, but their presence on the same page is not grounds for inferring a common origin. The path remains a starting point for checking decompression registration; stream ownership still needs to be confirmed at the actual call site.

## Recheck Addendum

A recheck weakened the earlier position that "empty streams are only related to missing input." The recheck did not establish that registry lookup is necessarily involved in every kind of empty stream, or that an empty stream necessarily comes with incomplete metadata; it showed only that an empty result alone is not enough to skip checking the link between registration and retrieval.

The record was then reframed as two parallel questions.

1. If the symptom comes from compression registry lookup, first distinguish the registration operation from the lookup operation. Completed registration only means that a compression method class has been placed where it can be retrieved; it is no substitute for observing the lookup result.
2. If the symptom comes from empty stream state, first mark the point at which the empty stream was observed. Without that point in time, do not discuss whether it is a normal branch, a post-read state, or a difference before and after information handoff.
3. Only when both observations are in the same caller should we consider whether to address them in the same change. Similar names are not a reason to merge them.

This addendum also retracts an earlier implication: the decompression object cannot be described as the sole holder of the empty stream. That path is directly relevant to registration issues, but reader ownership, higher-level call order, and metadata handoff are not determined by the filename.

## The Old Split, Left in Place

The following passage reflects an early handling convention and is retained for readers still arriving via old links. It is obsolete.

> First confirm that the stream contains no readable content. If it is empty, immediately exclude it from the decompression registration scope; if the target compression method appears in the registry, lookup can be considered fine.

This passage contains two errors. The first equates the presence of an entry in the registry with the result of a subsequent retrieval. The second treats empty content as the cause of an empty stream. The former misses changes between the registered object and the lookup result; the latter stops the record at the point where the stage most needs to be identified.

It is still here because, at the time, there was no call record spanning registration, lookup, stream creation, and information handoff. Splitting the issue temporarily was originally intended to limit how much needed to be read; the mistake came later, when that temporary split was written up as though it were a lasting boundary.

## Constraints Set in Review

The review did not approve the wording "a matching compression method is enough to close this out." The items to verify should be recorded separately: what was passed in during registration, and what was retrieved during lookup. This constraint does not assume that object identity is necessarily preserved, or that the implementation necessarily copies or caches objects; it simply rules out using the method name in place of the lookup result.

The same constraint was applied to empty streams. The term empty stream state is not synonymous with incomplete streamed metadata. They may occur around the same caller, or have no direct relationship at all. For an empty stream, first record the observation stage; for metadata handoff, first record whether it happened before or after the empty stream observation. When the evidence is insufficient, the two can only be recorded side by side.

This round of decisions did not merge the two tracks into a single fix task. The retained convention is: record object relationships for registration issues and observation stages for empty stream issues; assess whether they share a common cause only once both are found in the same caller.

## Unresolved Points

We still lack a call record that shows the registration input, lookup result, and empty stream observation together. We also lack material showing which object holds the empty stream before metadata handoff and which holds it afterward.

This page can now be used to prevent the old split from spreading further, but it cannot support a complete conclusion about the decompression lifecycle. The next addendum should prioritize documenting actual observation points rather than replacing "empty" with more generalized wording.

# Compression Registration and Empty-Stream Decision Record

This page was originally just a narrow record on the decompression side. Later, someone continued investigating compression registry lookup from the old entry point, while someone else returned here because of empty stream state, so the original passages of reasoning were not cleared out. They record trade-offs made at different times: first putting the two terms together, then separating them too early, and finally writing out the registration object and empty-stream phase separately. The old wording still has value as a reference, but not all of it can be treated as the current decision.

`lib/zip/decompressor.rb` has remained in the record throughout. It is the starting point of the compression-method registration issue, not proof of ownership of the entire stream lifecycle. Early on, this was exactly where we went too far: we turned a place where checking could begin into the place to which all empty-stream phenomena should be traced back. Later additions did not delete this path; they only withdrew that overly strong meaning.

---

## 2023-06-23: First, keep the issue together

The two objects in the initial draft were compression registry lookup and empty stream state. They were placed on the same page not because a shared implementation had already been found, and not because the same call trace already existed at the time. The only reliable commonality then was that both problem descriptions would lead the reader to the vicinity of the decompression object, and both descriptions could easily be wrapped up with a seemingly reasonable sentence.

The hasty statement on the registration side was, "The method has already been registered, so there will be no problem with lookup later." The hasty statement on the empty-stream side was, "There is no content, so there is no state to track either." The initial draft explicitly did not adopt either of these statements as a conclusion.

The first decision was to record the registration action and the subsequent lookup action separately. The existence of a registration only shows that registration occurred; it does not automatically answer what the lookup returns, nor whether there is wrapping, substitution, or another object relationship in between. The initial draft had no evidence with which to determine these details, so it only listed them as open questions.

The second decision was that an empty stream must not disappear from the record merely because its content is empty. When an empty stream is observed, we should at least record which side of the metadata handoff the observation is on. This requirement was not yet specific enough at the time to identify the holder or the call order; it was simply intended to prevent "empty" from being directly translated into "no state."

The initial draft left behind a strong working assumption: empty streams most likely come from missing input and therefore have no direct relationship to compression-method lookup. At the time, this was only intended to narrow the reading scope and was not written as an interface rule. It was precisely this assumption that later caused an unnecessary fork.

## Two short notes beside the initial draft

There were also two short, undeveloped notes beside the original record, worded much like temporary markers from that time.

- Do not look only at the method name.
- Do not look only at content length.

The reasons for leaving these two lines were more specific than they might seem. The first targets the compression method visible in the registry; that visibility can only help locate the registration side and cannot replace checking the result returned by the lookup. The second targets the surface appearance of an empty stream; a length of zero can describe the observation, but cannot tell us whether the stream has not yet been established, has already been fully read, or is currently near an information handoff.

At the time, these two sentences were not turned into operational steps. On the one hand, no call snippets had yet been seen that were sufficient to support a complete sequence; on the other, spelling them out too fully would mislead readers into thinking that all decompression paths had to pass through the same set of states. What remained was a narrower safeguard against mistakes: names cannot stand in for either object relationships or the stage of observation.

## The Old Assignment Practice After the First Draft

Early discussions assigned the two types of issues to different areas: compression registry lookup stayed on the decompression side, while empty stream state was left to the higher-level reading side. This arrangement was initially a convenience for communication. The registration issue already had a clear path name, while an empty stream looked more like a result left by the caller; separating the two gave readers at the time a quick stopping point.

The problem was not the temporary separation, but that later records described this assignment as a technical boundary. As a result, some people would see empty content and then skip over compression method registration entirely; others would see a compression method in the registry and stop paying attention to the subsequent lookup operation.

This page preserves that assignment practice to explain the gaps that occasionally appear in old defect descriptions: some records contain only a method name, without a lookup result; others say only "the stream is empty", without identifying the stage at which it was observed to be empty. These are not two complete chains of evidence, but partial notes left at the time from different entry points.

---

## Deprecated: Ending the Investigation Based on Entries and Empty Content

The old approach below is retained in its original location. It was once used as a quick way to handle these issues, but no longer applies.

> First confirm that the stream has no readable content. If it is empty, exclude it directly from the scope of decompression registration; if the target compression method appears in the registry, lookup can be considered normal.

This approach collapsed two different things into a judgment about the result.

An entry in the registry, the name of a compression method, and the object obtained by a lookup operation are not descriptions at the same level. The existence of an entry only means that tracing can begin on the registration side; it does not automatically mean that the lookup operation has been performed, much less establish which method class was retrieved. The old approach would therefore mistakenly record "seeing a name" as "the relationship has been confirmed".

Empty content is not the cause of an empty stream either. A stream can be observed as empty after it is created, and it can also leave different information states before and after metadata handoff. By stopping as soon as it saw no content, the old approach left the most important stage information out of the record.

The reason this old approach has not been deleted is not to preserve a shortcut that can still be followed. Old pages, old issue descriptions, and personal notes will still lead here through terms such as "registry" and "empty content". With the paragraph retained, readers can at least see at which step it turned a temporary division into a conclusion.

## 2024-01-01: The Review Did Not Support the Old Assumption

The follow-up review did not identify a single overarching cause that could explain all empty streams, nor did it conclude that "every kind of empty stream triggers registry lookup". What it overturned was the certainty in the old assumption: empty input does not establish that the lookup operation did not occur; a compression method being visible in the registry also does not establish that the expected result was necessarily obtained afterward.

This changed the order in which information was recorded. For registration-related behavior, first document the object passed in during registration separately from the object obtained during lookup. For empty-stream-related behavior, first record whether the observation occurred before or after metadata handoff; if this cannot be confirmed, explicitly leave it blank, rather than filling in missing input or incomplete metadata as the cause.

The review also forced the page to withdraw an implicit assumption: `lib/zip/decompressor.rb` cannot be treated as the only location holding the empty stream. This path sits alongside the object relationships involved in decompression registration, but reader ownership, when the stream is created, when it is read, and when information is handed off still depend on the actual call site. This change in wording is more useful than drawing a separate global lifecycle diagram, because the available material does not cover all the nodes that diagram would require.

At this stage, the decision was not to merge the two types of issues, but to change the minimum information recorded for each. The registration track must include at least the two actions of registration and lookup; the empty-stream track must include at least the observation stage. Without these two kinds of minimum information, assessments are no longer framed as directions for a fix.

## 2024-01-02: Review Notes

One comment from the review was retained: do not turn "the same compression method was found" into a conclusion about object relationships. Compression methods, registry entries, and lookup return values are at different levels. This comment did not ask for object identity, copying behavior, or caching behavior to be invented on the page; on the contrary, it required these unobserved details to remain undetermined.

The empty-stream section was narrowed in the same way. The review did not accept the substitution "empty stream state is incomplete streamed metadata". The two can appear near the same caller, but an empty stream is an observed state, while metadata handoff is a point that needs to be located; without the timing and call relationships, one term cannot stand in for the other.

The brief conclusions left after the review were:

- Look at what is passed in for registration, and what is retrieved for lookup.
- Check where an empty stream was observed, and do not simply supply a cause for how it arose.
- Discuss whether to share handling only when the two tracks meet at the same caller.

These sentences do not encompass every kind of reader, entry stream, or central record. They only correct this page's own earlier leaps: from names to object relationships, and from empty results to judgments about causes.

---

## Empty-Stream Review Record: What Is Missing Is the Location, Not More Adjectives

An empty stream had been treated as a shortcut to the explanation "there is no content to decompress". During the review, what could not actually be answered was not the phenomenon of emptiness itself, but where it occurred. When an empty stream is observed, without knowing whether it was just created, has already been read to completion, is ready for metadata handoff, or has already been saved by the caller, it is impossible to determine who should continue investigating this state.

The page was therefore later changed to start by adding observation labels. Labels can be "just observed to be empty", "observed to be empty before metadata handoff" or "observed to be empty after handoff". These are not enumeration interfaces, nor do they mean that each label will lead to a separate fix; they simply prevent logs or notes from writing up a timing question as a question of cause.

Someone proposed treating all empty streams as incomplete streamed metadata, on the grounds that both may occur around streaming reads. This proposal was not adopted. It was rejected not because the two are necessarily unrelated, but because this substitution would lose the lifecycle issue of the empty stream itself: even when the metadata is ultimately complete, it may still be necessary to know when the stream became empty; when the metadata is incomplete, empty content alone cannot determine the stage at which it arose either.

This round did not resolve reader ownership. It left only a narrower decision: without a call snippet, do not draw conclusions about the owner. The implication in the old wording that the decompression object was the sole owner has now been explicitly withdrawn.

## Retained legacy approach A: Confirm registration by method name

The old approach first checked whether the target compression method appeared in the registry, then recorded the result as "registry is ready". This wording can show that a particular name was once seen, but cannot show what the lookup path returned. It has been deprecated.

This passage is still retained because historical records sometimes contain only the method name. When reading such old records, interpret them as registration-side leads, not as corroborating evidence that lookup succeeded. The old text lacks a returned object; later readers should not fill in an unobserved relationship on its behalf.

## Retained legacy approach B: Stop tracking after encountering empty content

Another old approach was to stop further checks when the stream contained no content, on the assumption that there was no need to continue examining metadata handoff. This approach has also been deprecated. It only indicates that the observation point at the time saw empty content, not what states the stream passed through before and after that point.

This old approach and the assumption that "the empty stream comes from missing input" reinforced each other: the former stopped the record at empty content, while the latter supplied a reason for stopping. After review, neither can continue to serve as a stopping condition. If the stage is unknown, write that the stage is unknown; do not use a possible source as a substitute for the missing record of where it occurred.

## Retained legacy approach C: Treat the two lines of investigation as two boundaries

Initially, leaving registry lookup to the decompression side and empty stream state to the higher-level reading side made the division of work seem very clear. This was understandable as a temporary communication arrangement, but it is no longer a technical judgment.

Whether the two types of observations should be combined does not depend on whether a page mentions both, nor on whether both appear in the names of decompression-related issues. The actual adjacency between registration, lookup, stream creation, or metadata handoff within the same caller needs to be seen. Without this relationship, continuing to record them separately is more accurate than forcing a claim that they share an origin.

---

## 2025-05-21: Turn old conclusions into verifiable requirements

As of this addendum, the registration side finally needs a clearly identified interface point. The preceding layers of historical material have already shown that looking only at the compression method name is not enough, looking only at registry entries is not enough, and describing the lookup result with an unconfirmed generic term is not enough either. The relationship between the registration action and the lookup action should be stated directly, rather than continuing to use old phrasing such as "possibly the same" or "can usually be retrieved".

The current requirement is: Zip::Decompressor.register stores a compression method class that find_by_compression_method returns unchanged.

This requirement covers only the method class relationship between registration and lookup. It does not define empty stream state, does not determine whether metadata handoff is complete, and does not address reader ownership. It is included here to provide a verifiable reference point for the decompression registration issue, while avoiding further use of conclusions from the registration side to explain empty streams.

The current decision on empty streams remains narrow in scope. An empty stream is an independent lifecycle observation; the observation phase should be included when recording it. If the phase is unknown, it cannot be escalated to incomplete streamed metadata, nor can it be used to infer that compression registry lookup did not occur. This decision does not require all callers to produce the same kind of log, nor does it require a single fix for all empty streams.

The diagram below shows only the two recording branches currently accepted on this page, not a complete runtime flow, and it does not imply that the two branches necessarily intersect.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Registration" as registered
  state "Lookup" as lookup
  state "Returned object" as returned
  state "Empty stream observation" as empty
  state "Before metadata handoff" as before_handoff
  state "After metadata handoff" as after_handoff

  [*] --> registered
  registered --> lookup
  lookup --> returned
  [*] --> empty
  empty --> before_handoff
  empty --> after_handoff
```

Registration, lookup and the returned object in the diagram belong to the track recording the compression method class relationship; the empty stream observation and the stages on either side of handoff belong to the state identification track. The diagram does not show who holds the reader, nor does it show the full process of stream setup and closure, because the material on this page is insufficient to establish factual links between those nodes.

## 2025-05-22: Items retained after review

The old division was not reinstated after the review. Verification of the registration issue still starts near `lib/zip/decompressor.rb`, but that path is no longer taken to indicate ownership of the empty stream. The empty-stream issue still starts by asking which side of metadata handoff the observation occurred on, but observing an empty stream is no longer taken to mean that information must be missing.

The two threads can remain on this page, and the reason is clearer than it was early on: for a time, they shared the same flawed way of recording findings. The old records jumped straight from names to object relationships and from empty results to causes; the current decisions block these two leaps separately. Whether they share an implementation-level cause still has to be answered by the specific callers.

This page is adjacent to the interface topics in DOC-11, but it does not include other interface forms. The current page only preserves the historical distinctions between compression method registration, lookup results, and empty-stream observations; adding more objects would recreate an overall picture that appears complete but is not actually supported by call relationships.

## Questions still on this page

reader ownership has not yet been settled. The existing material can only confirm that the decompression side is the starting point for investigating the registration issue, not which object creates, retains, hands off, or closes the empty stream. If call records are added next time, they should first specify the actual caller, the observation point, and the state observed at the time, then explain which old claim they correct.

Another unresolved item is whether any caller continues passing empty stream state along as a normal branch rather than immediately ending the read. Without this information, empty streams cannot uniformly be described as abnormal, nor can they uniformly be described as a state that can be ignored.

Finally, no path showing the registered object, the object returned by lookup, and the empty-stream observation together has yet been recorded. Its absence does not affect the current registration requirements; it limits this page's ability to determine whether the two threads share an origin, when the stream changes, and what the ownership relationships are.

---

## Appendix of old examples

### Old example: Checking only the name after registration

The old record once stated "Seeing the target compression method name is enough to consider lookup complete". This example is outdated. The name can help locate the registration point, but it cannot replace the object returned by the lookup. This example is retained to explain why historical entries sometimes contain only the compression method and no result object.

### Old example: No longer marking handoff after an empty stream

Another old example stopped tracking once the content was empty, so it left no record of the metadata handoff location. This example is also outdated. It cannot prove that an empty stream necessarily involves incomplete information; it only shows that recording stopped once empty content appeared.

### Old example: Assigning two terms to two sides

The early text treated compression registry lookup as a decompression-side issue and empty stream state as a higher-level reading-side issue. This division is no longer used as a boundary. It remains in the appendix because some old links lead into this page based on that incorrect division.

These old examples should not be copied into new investigations. Their remaining value is to help readers recognize whether the old text actually captured only a name, a registration action, a lookup result, or an empty-stream observation at a particular stage.

# Decryption and Streamed Metadata Proposal

For this round, frozen-string decryption and incomplete streamed metadata are covered in the same evaluation draft, but are not treated as the same failure. The former concerns decryption reads after the caller passes in or retains a string; the latter concerns whether the reader can report its state when the streaming input has not yet supplied all the metadata. Both involve lifecycle, but they do not necessarily have the same starting point for investigation.

Start with `lib/zip/file.rb` to review the existing call names and adjacent objects. Use it to read the code and check historical behavior; don't start by assigning implementation ownership based on the path. Evaluation records should retain: the Ruby string settings used, the minimal entry point that triggers the read, and whether the metadata is complete before and after the read. Don't generalize from one successful open to every case.

There are two candidate approaches. The first is to keep a reproducible sample for each, then decide whether shared interface documentation is needed; the second is to put them directly under one set of read rules. The preference is for the first approach, because it has not yet been established whether incomplete metadata is a reader-side state, an upstream input state, or the result of the caller ending the stream early.

Provisional withdrawal criteria: the samples cannot reliably distinguish between these two kinds of cases, or the caller's original use of strings and streaming is changed to obtain a result. If that happens, do not expand interface commitments further; retain only the observations already made.

# Decryption and Streamed Metadata Proposal

The previous draft placed the two topics side by side to avoid missing boundaries in the read lifecycle. That presentation could easily suggest a shared starting point for a fix. Set that assumption aside first during review. `lib/zip/file.rb` remains the starting point for checking call names, but file location cannot substitute for confirming the relationships between objects.

The evaluation now has two separate records.

- frozen-string decryption: record only the entry points actually used for decryption reads in a Ruby environment with frozen string literals enabled. Check whether the read can complete and whether the caller needs to copy or modify strings to work around the issue.
- incomplete streamed metadata: record only when the metadata from the streaming input is not yet complete. The record must specify the observation point: whether missing fields were found before the read began, during the read, or after the read ended; without this detail, the behavior cannot be attributed to the read interface.

Both records share one constraint: the samples must preserve the original call order. Do not first collect the stream into another form of input just to produce a success or failure, or first turn the string into a mutable object. Results obtained that way only show that the alternative call works; they do not establish the boundaries of the original entry point.

The second candidate approach in the earlier draft was to write unified rules directly. We are not adopting it yet. The benefit is that callers only need to look in one place; the cost is that it would conflate "metadata has not yet arrived" and "decryption read failed" into a single externally visible state. Even if both occur in the same regression sample, their results should still be recorded separately.

What needs to be added this round is a minimal description for each sample, not more scenarios: Ruby string settings, the read entry point, whether the streamed metadata was complete at the time, and the result. If a record can only say "failed" and cannot say where it happened, leave it out of the interface documentation.

The withdrawal criteria have also been narrowed: if reproducing the issue requires changing the call order, or the stage at which metadata was missing fields cannot be determined, stop using that sample to draw conclusions about the interface. Retain it as a sample for further investigation, and do not use it to add compatibility commitments.

It is still undecided whether the two samples will ultimately need the same caller-facing documentation. That decision should wait until their results can be compared.

# Decryption and Streaming Metadata Proposal

The shared pilot framework left by the old draft can still be used, but it should no longer be understood as a shared interface proposal. The work item now has only one purpose: to let callers determine separately what their samples actually show when decryption reads are incomplete and when streamed metadata is incomplete. Both types of issue can occur during a read; that is not enough to prove that they should be handled at the same layer.

The earliest draft only required retaining the string setting, the read entry point, and the result. That requirement was too loose: two records with the same result might differ in where they stopped—one while the input had not yet provided complete metadata, and the other in the decryption path. The "stage" field added later was not intended to add formatting to the record; it was intended to prevent input state from being written up as an interface result.

`lib/zip/file.rb` continues to serve as a cross-reference point. It can help verify the call name and nearby code, but cannot by itself answer who owns a particular lifecycle decision. Once the file is located, record the actual entry point in the sample first; if the sample and the name in the file do not match, retain the discrepancy and do not use path proximity to fill in the inference.

## Boundary Between the Two Records

**Decryption reading.** The record must retain whether Ruby frozen string literals are enabled and whether the caller changed the string to work around the issue. Copying the string, rewriting parameters, or switching to a different read form should each be recorded separately as variants; none can replace the result of the original call. The success criterion should also be kept narrow: verify only the target read action, without extrapolating from a single read to other decryption, write, or archive-update behavior.

**Streaming metadata.** The record must state whether the metadata was still incomplete at the time of observation, and whether that determination was made before the read started, during the read, or after it ended. Without a stage, "incomplete" cannot distinguish between the input not having arrived in full and the stream having been consumed or terminated early somewhere. This record does not use the success or failure of the decryption sample as evidence.

This split also corrects the old draft's tendency to assume that "the unified rule can be written first." A unified description may look simpler, but it would lead callers to put waiting for more input and handling decryption reads in the same branch. At this point, retain only a shared record format; do not promise a shared handling strategy.

## Currently Confirmable Read Sample

For the frozen-string-literal case, the determination should be based on concrete read capability rather than an inference about string ownership:

Zip::DecryptedIo can read a byte successfully when Ruby frozen string literals are enabled.

This statement covers only the case of a successful byte read. It does not replace the streamed metadata record, nor does it mean that every caller can skip checking its own entry point. The entry point used and the string setting should still be written next to the sample; otherwise, later readers cannot tell whether the observation still corresponds to the same type of call.

## Options Retained in Review

Three ways to close this out were considered.

1. Immediately define both cases as rules for the same read interface.
2. Keep only the minimum sample for each, then compare them after the caller results are complete.
3. Record input state and decryption reads separately first, then let the maintainer decide whether a shared explanation is needed.

The first is not adopted: the available material is insufficient to classify the timing of metadata arrival as decryption behavior. The second risks leaving the two samples stalled separately, and would also make it hard later to tell whether they used the same entry point. The third is adopted here. It does not require the two cases to be merged in the end; it requires that, if merging is to be discussed, the stage at which each result occurred can first be identified.

The historical records for ARC-202 show that the results available so far are enough to enter review, but the conditions for withdrawal still need to be confirmed. Here, withdrawal does not deny the recorded reading phenomenon; it means no longer elevating samples without stage information into an interface commitment. For string samples, if obtaining a result requires first copying, rewriting, or replacing the original call, their eligibility as evidence for the original entry point should also be withdrawn.

ARC-219 remain as the investigation entry point for incomplete streamed metadata. What needs to be added there is not more generic description, but each sample's metadata state and observation stage. If all we know is that "the stream did not complete," we still cannot determine how the read layer should respond.

The macOS form of that incomplete local metadata now has a caller-facing result. A streamed archive with incomplete local metadata from the macOS form raises Zip::Error instead of yielding an entry. The raised error names the incomplete local metadata, for example as local-header metadata or as bit 3. That case stays separate from a data-descriptor entry, whose error identifies the InputStream or the local-header metadata boundary.

## Deliverable and Open Items

The final write-up should retain two independent sets of sample fields:

| Object | Must retain | Do not infer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| frozen-string decryption | String setting, actual read entry point, byte-read result | Conclusions about other decryption or write paths |
| incomplete streamed metadata | Metadata state, observation stage, corresponding entry point | Conclusions about decryption reads |

If the same caller encounters both at the same time, they can be listed side by side in one record, but each set of fields must still be filled in separately. The cost is a longer record; the benefit is that, during review, one side can be removed without breaking the meaning of the other.

Two items remain unconfirmed and stay sample notes rather than interface results: first, which callers still use frozen-string entry points that need checking; second, whether other streamed metadata samples can reliably identify the stage at which a missing item appears. Those open sample notes do not withdraw the caller-facing result already recorded for the macOS form, and path navigation is still not a conclusion about ownership.

# Input Stream Error Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

Start by checking whether an entry has already been retrieved from the input stream. Don't conflate the state just after the archive object was opened with the state after switching entries. In the May notes, `lib/zip/input_stream.rb` was treated as the first place to check: the issue report covered both stream size and differences before and after `get_next_entry`. Not enough call examples were retained at the time, and the issue title alone is not enough to determine whether the cause was on the reader side, the caller side, or in the input file.

Start with the following troubleshooting sequence:

```text
Reader obtains InputStream
|
+-- No entry retrieved yet
|   +-- Record the call site and the properties read at that point
|   +-- Do not substitute values from a later entry for the current observation
|
+-- Already called get_next_entry
|   +-- Record whether the caller saved the returned entry
|   +-- Compare the read results before and after the switch
|
+-- Starting point mentions split signature
    +-- Stop interpreting it as ordinary single-file input
    +-- Record the original input source and invocation method
```

The old working rule was "as long as the stream object exists, size should be readable." This rule was meant to point the person on duty to the input stream layer first; it was not a verified interface guarantee. It lacked counterexamples for the path where no entry had been selected, and it did not specify which layer should reject split archive signatures.

When split signature rejection occurs, first confirm which call entry point produced the error. If all you know is that the user saw a rejection, you cannot infer that the central records have already been read, or classify the issue as a size calculation error. First, keep a record of where the input stream was created, where the first entry was retrieved, and whether the failure occurred before or after that retrieval. If the sequence can't be reconstructed, record it as "call order unconfirmed"; don't fill in a definitive timeline.

The visible file-level starting point is still `lib/zip/input_stream.rb`. This is a suitable place to check the state exposed by the input stream around entry transitions; to establish where split archives are actually handled, you need to continue tracing outward from the call in question.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Input Stream Anomaly Boundaries

This record initially covered only reports that "stream size looks unstable". During a later review, split signature rejection also appeared at the same set of entry points; the two were grouped together because investigators would start by looking at the input stream in both cases, not because they had been proven to originate from the same piece of logic.

## Early Guidance Retained

The original guidance in May was: once a stream object is created, size should be treated as state that can be read directly. This was a simplification to make communication easier at the time, and is no longer appropriate as a basis for troubleshooting decisions. It did not distinguish between cases where no entry had been obtained yet, an entry had already been obtained, and the caller had cached an old object between two entry objects.

The steps in the original record are still useful, but their order needs to be specified: first ask the caller "where was the last `get_next_entry` call", then check whether the property being read comes from stream or entry. Without these two points, it is impossible to determine whether the observation reflects the current state or a reference left over from the previous entry.

```text
A size anomaly is reported
|
+-- The only description is "size is wrong"
|   |
|   +-- Ask for the call location
|   +-- Ask for the sequence involving get_next_entry
|   +-- Ask whether the entry selected at that time had changed
|
+-- A call snippet has been provided
|   |
|   +-- The read occurs before the first get_next_entry
|   |   +-- Record it under the branch where no entry has been selected
|   |
|   +-- The read occurs after get_next_entry
|       +-- Verify whether the reader still holds the entry returned by this call
|
+-- The snippet also includes split signature
    |
    +-- Record the two separately first
    +-- Do not use the size anomaly to explain the signature rejection
```

"Record the two separately" here does not mean creating two incident reports. It only requires separating the visible symptoms into columns within the same troubleshooting material: one column for the entry-selection sequence, and one for the location of the signature rejection. The former is a state boundary, and the latter is an input-format boundary. When neither column has evidence yet, prioritize filling in entry-point details rather than adding speculation.

## September Review Addendum

During the review, the entry-point names around `lib/zip/input_stream.rb` were examined again. What can be confirmed is that issue naming has consistently grouped `Zip::InputStream` with stream, entry, and `get_next_entry`; what cannot be confirmed is whether every historical call followed the same read path. The earlier conclusion that "all size reports come from the same calling pattern" has been crossed out, and the original conclusion is retained so that later readers can understand why only one branch was examined at the time.

The deprecated troubleshooting sequence is as follows:

1. Immediately inspect the compressed data when size is empty or missing;
2. If split signature is also present, treat it as corroborating evidence of compressed-data corruption;
3. Work backward from the final exception and infer that an entry must have been selected along the way.

The problem with these three steps is not that they are entirely unusable, but that they skip object state. Compressed data, split input, and entry selection may all be worth investigating, but without sequence information, they cannot serve as evidence for one another.

After the review, first make two brief notes:

| What needs to be recorded | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Where `Zip::InputStream` is created | Distinguish object creation from an entry having been selected |
| Where the first `get_next_entry` occurs | Establish the time boundary for subsequent reads |
| The most recent read before the failure | Determine whether split signature appeared before the entry read |
| Whether the caller continues to reuse an old entry | Avoid treating an old object as the current selection |

Do not invent line numbers or filenames just to fill in the table. If they cannot be obtained, write "not provided" and stop attributing the cause any further.

## split signature Branch

A report of split signature rejection should start from the point where the rejection occurs, rather than first reframing it as "failed halfway through reading". If the failure occurs before the first `get_next_entry`, the entry-selection branch does not yet apply; if the failure occurs after an entry has been obtained, that only shows that the call sequence contains both events, and does not by itself establish that the signature check depends on that entry.

Follow this tree when handling these reports:

```text
split signature rejection occurs
|
+-- The failure point is visible during input stream creation
|   +-- Record the input source
|   +-- Do not record a conclusion about entry size
|
+-- The failure point is near the first get_next_entry
|   +-- Preserve the call order before and after it
|   +-- Check whether an entry object has already been obtained
|
+-- Rejection is reported only after an entry has been obtained
|   +-- Retain the selected entry's name or how the caller stores it (if available)
|   +-- Do not turn "obtained" into "caused the rejection"
|
+-- The failure point is unknown
    +-- Record only the rejection
    +-- Return to the call entry point to obtain a snippet
```

The stopping condition here is simple: if the order of the rejection and the first entry retrieval cannot be established, do not continue assessing size. This is not because the two are necessarily unrelated, but because the current material is insufficient to connect them into a causal chain.

## Counterexamples Retained from the Review

A counterexample was raised during the review: a call to Fang Ke can save the input stream first, then obtain an entry at a different location; if only the final line that reads size is captured, the record will incorrectly describe "the object already exists" as "an entry has been selected". This counterexample changed the order of checks in the document. Now, look for state transitions first, then property reads.

Another counterexample concerns split signature. When a report contains only the rejection message, investigators tend to attribute it to input stream reading; however, the message itself does not identify the layer at which the failure occurred. Unless a call snippet or runtime record identifies the location, it can only be treated here as an input-format signal that requires branching.

## Current Working Sequence

1. Write down the relative order of object creation and the first `get_next_entry`.
2. Mark whether an entry had already been selected when size was read.
3. If split signature rejection is also present, mark its location separately.
4. Revisit `lib/zip/input_stream.rb` only once a clear call sequence is available; if there is no sequence, obtain the caller's supporting material first.
5. If the two symptoms come from different entry points, close out the records separately rather than forcing them together.

Still unconfirmed: whether the specific rejection point for split signature is consistent across different input forms; whether any callers reused entry objects in the historical reports. Until these two gaps are filled, do not reinstate the old claim that "size and signature rejection share the same cause" as a conclusion.

# Input Stream Exception Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

Older records of input stream issues were scattered across different batches: some people started with size, others started with split signature rejection, and some left only a short snippet of calls before and after `get_next_entry`. They were later consolidated here, not to find a single root cause for the two symptoms, but to ensure that troubleshooting first puts object state, failure timing, and input format back into their respective contexts.

The current starting point is still to trace back from `lib/zip/input_stream.rb`. This file can help confirm how reads relate to the input stream and entry selection; it is not a complete map of the split archive processing chain. When investigating an actual report, you must start with the sequence preserved by the caller, then decide whether you need to return here.

## 2023-05: The Earliest Note

The earliest note contained only a simple assumption: once the stream object was created, size should already have a stable meaning. At the time, this assumption could explain one category of reports that "read results differed from expectations", so troubleshooting focused directly on stream properties.

The original text did not distinguish between three points: immediately after the input stream was created, when an entry was first obtained, and after switching to the next entry. Nor did it record whether the caller read immediately or only after passing the stream elsewhere. It treated "the object exists" and "an entry has been selected" as the same state, which is precisely what later counterexamples disproved.

The shortest troubleshooting path left from that investigation is still preserved below. It reflects the working approach used at the time, and should not be treated as the current stopping condition:

```text
Observe a size anomaly
  -> Open the input stream-related code
  -> Check size
  -> Check compressed data
```

This path omitted `get_next_entry`. If the call snippet does not include that call, compressed data cannot be used to explain size; if the call snippet already includes that call, you still cannot skip checking whether the entry has switched. The old path has not been deleted, because early reports did use it to gather material, and follow-up investigations need to know which information was not asked for in the first place.

## First Marginal Note: Record the State First, Not the Exception Name

An operational reminder was later added on a side page: even if a report only says "size is wrong", the first line must record the last state transition. This reminder was initially intended only to reduce back-and-forth clarification, and was not a new conclusion about the interface.

The available reporting format is very constrained:

```text
InputStream creation: known / unknown
First get_next_entry: before reading / after reading / unknown
Object being read: stream / entry / unknown
Could the entry have already switched: yes / no / unknown
```

"Unknown" is not a synonym for a to-do item. It means that the current investigation stops here: without the call sequence, a property value cannot be interpreted as an error, nor can you assume that an entry has already been selected just because execution did not fail immediately.

At the time, someone suggested continuing to trace all unknowns down to the archive file itself. This suggestion was not adopted. The input file may matter, but it cannot replace the call sequence. First clarify whether the object has already passed through `get_next_entry`, so that you know whether to investigate the file, the entry, or the caller next.

## 2023-06: The first counterexample

The first clear counterexample came from a calling pattern that retained the object. After the input stream is created, an entry is not necessarily selected immediately; the caller may also retain the returned object after a selection and then let the input stream advance further. Looking at just one line containing a read statement collapses these different timing relationships into a single point.

The old statement "as long as there is a stream, size can be determined" was therefore marked as deprecated. It was deprecated not because all reads had been found to be incorrect, but because the statement erased the point in time at which the observation was made.

The revised manual check consists of two questions:

- Before the read, was the last call the one that created the input stream or `get_next_entry`?
- After the read, will the caller continue calling `get_next_entry` and treat the earlier entry as the current object?

The answers to these two questions cannot be inferred from the exception name. When snippets are missing, record only the answers to the questions; do not fill in "the entry is usually obtained first" as a fact.

There was also a minor unresolved question at the time: whether entry names needed to be saved consistently on the caller side to make it easier to associate read records with specific objects. This question was never split out into a separate change. It remains a related issue, but it does not affect branching by state here first.

## Old branch: Treating split signature as supporting evidence for size

An earlier round of investigation that same year placed split signature rejection under size exceptions. The wording at the time was: once signature rejection is seen, first assume that the read stream has gone off track around the size or compressed data, then investigate inward starting from the input stream.

This section is retained as a historical procedure:

```text
size looks abnormal
|
+-- split signature rejection is also present
|   +-- First assume the input has entered the normal read path
|   +-- Look for commonalities around size and compressed data
|
+-- No signature rejection
    +-- Continue examining entry reads
```

This tree is no longer applicable. The problem is not that "signature rejection is definitely unrelated to the input stream", but that "occurring together" does not establish the order of events. Signature rejection may occur before an entry is selected, or after the caller has already performed other actions. The old tree treated two terms in the same report as the same path, narrowing the investigation too early.

The stopping rule retained beside the old tree was also flawed: it required the person on duty to continue inspecting the archive contents if no commonality could be found. This is no longer done. If it is not possible to identify whether rejection occurred when the input stream was created, when the first entry was obtained, or at some later point, first stop making causal judgments and collect the calling pattern and the original failure location.

## 2023-09: Review notes

The September review again split the observations into two columns. The first column covers only entry state transitions; the second covers only when split signature rejection occurs. After this change, the previous record stating "the size anomaly already explains the signature rejection" no longer holds, and has been changed to "the two phenomena appear in the same report, but their relationship is unconfirmed".

The table used for the review is below. Its purpose is not to require every field every time, but to prevent inferences from being filled in when fields are missing:

| Observation | What may be recorded | Should not be recorded as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input stream creation | Call site known or unknown | An entry has already been selected |
| First `get_next_entry` | Before the read, after the read or unknown | The read must have succeeded |
| size read | Where it occurs, the object read from | The compressed data has been validated |
| split signature rejection | Where it occurs, the original call entry point | Caused by size |
| entry switch | Present, absent or unknown | The previous entry is still the current entry |

After the review, one decision was that the size branch would no longer connect directly to the split branch. They are listed side by side in the troubleshooting table, and their order may only be compared when the same call sequence is available. A report without a sequence can at most serve as material awaiting additional information, not as a basis for attributing both phenomena to a common cause.

## On-call addendum: Where a report first lands

The material most commonly received during on-call shifts is incomplete. Some callers provide only a single rejection, some only say "the size we got is wrong", and others paste an instance of `get_next_entry`. This incompleteness does not mean that the report is useless; it only determines where troubleshooting stops.

### A. Only a size description

First ask whether `get_next_entry` has already been executed. If the answer is unclear, record the object creation point, and stop interpreting the meaning of size. Do not switch to asking "what is the compression algorithm" to work around this gap, and do not assume that an entry has been selected based on whether the archive can be opened.

If the read is confirmed to have occurred after the first `get_next_entry`, then ask whether the reader was using the input stream itself or the previously returned entry. If the caller retained an entry object, subsequent changes to the stream position do not mean that the object automatically represents the current state. What is needed here is the relationship between the objects, not a guess about whether a particular value is good or bad.

### B. Only split signature rejection

First record the rejection verbatim as a failure signal related to the input format, and follow up on where the failure occurred. If the failure occurred around input stream creation, do not enter the entry size branch; if the failure occurred near the first `get_next_entry`, preserve the order of the calls before and after it; if the failure point is completely unknown, collect only the call entry point.

Do not write "rejection" as "data corruption." This page does not contain enough evidence to make that attribution. Nor should you write it the other way around as "signature check is working correctly," because both the invocation method and the input form may still affect what is observed.

### C. Both occur

Write two lines in chronological order rather than a single sentence saying "size anomaly accompanied split rejection". For example: first record which read produced size, then record where rejection occurred; if the order cannot be reconstructed, mark both lines as unknown. Discuss whether one phenomenon obscured the other only when the same call sequence can establish the order.

```text
Two phenomena in the same report
|
+-- Recoverable call order
|   |
|   +-- rejection before the first get_next_entry
|   |   +-- Handle the signature branch first; do not determine selected entry
|   |
|   +-- size read after get_next_entry
|   |   +-- Verify whether the read is of the stream or the stored entry
|   |
|   +-- Both positions are present
|       +-- Compare timing only; do not directly assign a shared cause
|
+-- Call order cannot be recovered
    +-- Split into two observations
    +-- Stop at the point for supplementing the call entry
```

The purpose of this tree is not to make every report go all the way to the end. Reaching "call order cannot be recovered" is already a valid stopping point; continuing to speculate inside the file will only disguise missing evidence as a conclusion.

## Withdrawn approaches

An earlier recommendation required the following: after detecting split signature rejection, first have the caller retry with regular archive input, then check whether size recovered. This recommendation is now marked as no longer applicable.

There are two reasons. First, retrying changes the input form, so it cannot show where the original rejection occurred. Second, even if the read result after the retry differs, it cannot answer whether the first call had already selected an entry. It turns troubleshooting into input replacement without preserving the original state boundary.

The old recommendation was not erased from the documentation because historical reports may indeed reference it. When an old record citing this recommendation is encountered, add "The input form has been replaced and cannot be used to determine the original call sequence", rather than rewriting the old report as if the current branch had already been followed at the time.

Another withdrawn practice was to directly ask the caller to read all fields of the entry when size had not been provided. This would usually provide more material, but it could also cause the caller to change its own workflow. Now, only the call order that actually occurred is required; if an execution snippet needs to be added, it should retain the entry point used by the issue, and should not trigger a separate entry switch just to collect fields.

## Meaning of a meeting excerpt

A review left a brief comment: first clarify "when the object becomes a readable entry context", then discuss the numbers. This is not asking us to attach new lifecycle terminology to the input stream, nor does it mean that all fields must be recorded every time. It simply corrects the earlier framing that equated the existence of a stream with an entry already having been selected.

Another reviewer pointed out that the failure message for split signature rejection is not enough on its own to identify the processing layer. This feedback changed how observations were recorded: from then on, signature rejection would no longer be attributed to a particular internal step unless a call snippet could show which action the failure occurred near.

The division of responsibilities after the review is not documented here. This document retains a decision sequence that the on-call investigator can follow; changes requiring coordination should still be handled in discussions of the specific calls and implementation.

## Current troubleshooting tree

For related reports now, start with observed behavior, not guesses.

```text
Start: The report involves InputStream, size or split signature rejection
|
+-- Does the report provide the call order?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Record the creation point of InputStream (if available)
|   |   +-- Record whether get_next_entry appears (if available)
|   |   +-- Record size and rejection separately
|   |   +-- Stop: Do not infer a causal relationship between the two
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Is size read before the first get_next_entry?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes: Record it as a state with no entry selected
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No: Confirm the object being read and the most recent entry switch
|       |
|       +-- Is there a split signature rejection?
|           |
|           +-- No: Finish recording the size branch
|           |
|           +-- Yes: Mark its position relative to creation and the first entry retrieval
|               |
|               +-- Position unknown: Stop attributing a common cause
|               |
|               +-- Position known: Compare only the order, and continue retaining both types of observations
```

"Record it as a state with no entry selected" means not copying the properties of a later entry back into the record, and not filling in the blanks with an entry object left over from the previous loop iteration. If the caller only needs to determine at this point whether reading can continue, first revisit the purpose of the call; this page does not require extra reads to produce an entry.

"Confirm the object being read" also cannot be reduced to checking the variable name. You need to confirm whether the caller is reading properties exposed by the input stream, the entry just returned, or a previously saved object. Continuing to use `entry` as the variable name does not prove that it still corresponds to the current selection.

"Mark the location" can at least be expressed in one of three ways: around the time the input stream is created, around the time of the first `get_next_entry`, or after the entry operation has completed. A lack of more precise timing does not prevent using these three categories; but do not invent a fourth category describing an internal processing stage.

## Current requirements

For size-related records, the current conclusion about the interface is limited to this sentence: Zip::InputStream reports nil size before an entry is selected and the selected entry's uncompressed size after get_next_entry.

This sentence only addresses what the input stream reports before and after entry selection, and does not replace the determination of whether to reject a split archive. During troubleshooting, if the observed size does not match this boundary, first revisit the call order and the object being read; if split signature rejection also occurs, retain a separate record of it based on the failure location. Do not extend the current requirements to mean "all archives will reject a split signature at the same point in time", as this page draws no such conclusion.

Current code tracing still starts at `lib/zip/input_stream.rb`. Only when a report has already described the object state and failure timing are there clear questions to guide the code investigation: whether the read occurred before entry selection, or after entry selection; whether rejection occurred earlier in the same call sequence. The file path alone cannot substitute for answers to these questions.

## Remaining side questions

Whether historical reports contain a pattern of "retrieving an entry first, then having another piece of code continue advancing the input stream" has not yet been systematically reviewed. This question affects the interpretation of the object being read, but the available material does not support describing it as general behavior.

Also, the actual call entry point for split signature rejection still needs to be filled in from specific reports. In future additions, prioritize adding the original call sequence, with no need to copy the entire archive contents onto this page. If new material shows rejection occurring at different locations, add samples under the corresponding branches, and do not rewrite old records to make them look as though they had been consistent all along.

## Appendix: Retained excerpts from earlier incidents

### Old example 1: Check the data directly when size is empty

The early excerpt said "when size is empty, first check whether the data is complete". At the time, this was meant to provide a starting point for vague reports, but now it can only serve as a historical entry point. It did not ask whether `get_next_entry` had already occurred, so it cannot be used to assess the state when no entry has been selected.

### Old example 2: Change the input and retry after signature rejection

The old example recommended replacing a potentially split input with a regular input and continuing to read. This changes the issue itself, so it cannot be used to preserve the timing of the original rejection. When historical compatibility is needed, you may note that a retry was made using this method, but must not present the retry result as the result for the original input.

### Notes not yet split out

The input stream creation point, entry selection point, and the way the caller stores the object are still the three types of evidence most commonly missing in each investigation. Here, we only retain their relationship to size and split signature; other archive lifecycle issues should be documented separately.

# Entry Encoding and Size Migration Notes

Start by recording these compatibility checks as two separate migration tracks: global encoding reset goes under the entry-name configuration path, and unknown local sizes under the local-size read path. The initial draft did not treat them as the same failure.

Legacy callers typically bring their own name-encoding settings into entry processing. During migration, first preserve where those settings are applied and the call order, then go to `lib/zip/entry.rb` to check the initialization and name checks for `Entry`. You can find `set_default_vars_values`, `check_name(name)`, and `initialize` directly here; start by reviewing these adjacent locations, and don't replace settings based on the issue name alone.

Keep size records separate to start with. When a local size is unknown, record what the entry point returned or threw on that invocation, and mark whether it happened before initialization, during initialization, or after the entry was readable. Reviewing name encoding is no substitute for this check.

The tentative rollback plan is to undo the name-setting changes introduced during migration and restore where the caller originally applied the settings; retain the size-check records rather than deleting them as part of the encoding rollback.

Still to add: whether there is another point between default-value initialization and name checking that reintroduces the old settings; the public entry points for unknown local sizes have not yet been mapped out.

# Entry Encoding and Size Migration Notes

The initial draft was right to keep the two tracks separate, but it scoped name settings too narrowly by treating them as local state within a single `Entry`. After reviewing `lib/zip/entry.rb`, the old steps still work as a starting point for reading: first look at `Entry`'s `initialize`, then at `set_default_vars_values`; name input passes through `check_name(name)`. But that no longer justifies assuming that name settings persist only within a single entry.

Keep two records for this migration.

**Name encoding**: First identify where the caller applies forced name-encoding settings. Don't change the defaults first and then trace back to the call sites; that can easily hide the original order in which settings were applied. Record the pre-migration setting location alongside the post-migration cleanup location. During review, process entry names twice in succession to see whether the previous setting still has an effect. The old note's claim that "checking only the first read is enough" no longer applies; it is retained here to show that cross-call cases were missed at the time.

**Local sizes**: unknown local sizes is no longer treated as a name-encoding counterexample. Record its results through its own public entry points, including at least: which stage of entry reading was in progress at the time, whether the result was a return value or an exception, and whether the entry object had finished initializing. In the `Entry` file, `time` and `file_type_is` can help locate the relevant sections, but they are no substitute for conclusions about sizes.

The handoff sequence between the old and new paths is as follows:

```text
Old: Caller retains name settings → Process one entry → Then let the next call determine the state
New: Preserve the source of the settings → Make the cleanup point explicit → Run consecutive name-processing checks
```

"Process one entry" in the diagram is not an in-file call graph; it is just the check sequence from the old migration record. Unknown sizes are not included in this arrow; record their observed results separately.

If the consecutive checks after migration show a discrepancy, roll back only the newly added cleanup wiring and restore where the caller originally applied the settings. Don't also change size handling to make the results look consistent. If the size issue still occurs, retain the original return value or exception content and continue checking the object state around `initialize`.

Still unconfirmed: whether complete and incomplete streaming metadata can already be distinguished before the name check when local sizes are unknown. This review did not resolve that question.
