# Entry Encoding and Size Migration Notes

This note was originally dug up during a migration for legacy callers: the name-encoding setting and the unknown local-size behavior appeared close together, so they were documented on the same page. The early steps started by looking at `lib/zip/entry.rb`, because `Entry`'s `initialize`, `set_default_vars_values`, and `check_name(name)` are all here; the judgment at the time was that tracing defaults and name checks was enough to decide where the migration needed changes.

That judgment still stands, but is no longer complete. It is useful for finding where to start reading, but not for defining how long the name setting remains in effect. In particular, the old note's "checking only the first read is enough" was later disproved by counterexamples involving consecutive calls: a normal name on the first entry does not mean later calls did not inherit the forced setting from the previous call.

The order on the old migration ticket is still useful as a reference; it just has one additional cleanup step in the middle:

```text
Old path
Caller sets name encoding
        |
        v
Process current Entry
        |
        v
Let the next call decide for itself whether to keep carrying the setting

Path retained after migration
Caller sets name encoding → Finish current use → Clear global setting → Process next Entry
```

This diagram is not the call relationship inside `Entry`, nor does it indicate that unknown local sizes pass through name checking. It only shows where the migration wiring should be split: the source of the name setting stays in the caller; the entry file is used to check the adjacent locations for initialization, default values, and name validation; the cleanup action cannot depend on whether a particular `Entry` instance is still in hand.

During review, first note the location where the legacy caller forcibly sets name encoding. Next confirm that the migration actually performs cleanup after the current use ends, rather than moving the setting into default-value code such as `set_default_vars_values`. Then use one later name-processing operation as a check: later processing should not continue using that setting merely because the previous call forced name encoding. The wording to retain here is:

> Zip.reset! clears Zip.force_entry_names_encoding so a forced entry-name encoding does not leak across calls.

This also corrects the draft's claim that reset should be treated as an internal entry cleanup operation. `Zip.reset!` handles cross-call residue; `check_name(name)` remains a local inspection point for name input, and the two should not substitute for each other. If the migration commit only changes name checking and does not handle the global setting, still trace the setting's source back through the old path.

Continue checking unknown local sizes separately. An earlier record suggested finishing the encoding review first and then attaching the size observation to the same result; that step is now marked obsolete. Normal name encoding does not indicate that the local size is available, and vice versa. When the size is unknown, record only what is actually returned or thrown through the current public entry point, and note whether, at that time, the object was before `initialize`, was in initialization, or had already entered a readable state. Do not interpret the size result as encoding residue just to make the migration record look tidy.

Within the file, you can still use several locations as quick anchors: `module Zip` and `class Entry` confirm the reading scope; `set_default_vars_values` is for checking the initial state; `check_name(name)` is for checking name input; `time` and `file_type_is` are only auxiliary anchors when identifying entry state. There is not enough material here to expand these declarations into a complete implementation diagram for size reads, so the old page did not add that diagram.

Handle rollback separately as well. If the new cleanup point prevents an existing caller from preserving its original setting order, remove the newly added `Zip.reset!` wiring and restore the caller's original setting location, while retaining the review record for consecutive calls. Do not delete the observed results for unknown local sizes as part of the rollback, and do not change name checking to hide the size behavior. After rollback, still recheck whether the later name processing is affected by the previous setting; otherwise, you have only returned to the old path without showing whether the old path is safe.

One unfinished edge remains on this page: when the local size is unknown, the question of which public entry point can first distinguish incomplete streaming metadata from other states has not yet been turned into a stable procedure. Follow-up investigation can start near initialization around `Entry`, but do not apply the name-encoding conclusion to this path prematurely.

# Entry Name Lookup Trial Log

The review still starts near `lib/zip/filesystem.rb`. This rb module is a navigation point left by the earlier investigation, useful for revisiting where the filesystem facade meets the entry name; the call relationships still need to be confirmed by following the references used at the time. The filename was not treated as evidence that any particular part of the implementation belonged to it.

The input records are kept separate. The first group uses a minimal but real directory tree, passing candidate paths to the lookup one by one to check whether each candidate location can still reach the target entry. The requirements recorded in ARC-205 also call for checking at this granularity, rather than merely confirming that a directory can be listed. The second group retains the sorted-read setup: ARC-222 points to the state anomaly that appeared after `no-rewrite sorted reads`; at this stage, first inspect the state and buffer contents before and after reading, without conflating it with path syntax as the same failure cause.

This review yielded the following conclusion about name syntax:

Zip::File lookup normalizes an entry name written with backslashes so the same entry is readable with forward slashes.

Therefore, in the directory-tree experiment, backslashes and forward slashes are not two independent reachability rules; they are two input forms for the same entry-name lookup. Candidate paths should still be kept separately, because the directory hierarchy, missing nodes, and target entry do not disappear as a result of this normalization step. The record also does not use "directory can be listed" as a substitute for "the specified entry is readable."

No conclusion about rewriting was drawn from this for the sorted-read group. The check here still starts with the state and buffer bytes before and after reading; if the state anomaly appears only after sorting, in the next round hold the same entry-name input fixed and switch only whether sorting is applied. If both read orders reproduce it, go back to entry-state handling and check whether a common path exists.

This round leaves two points for continued investigation: the minimal directory tree must cover candidate paths where the target entry is in a deep directory; the sorted-read test must retain an unsorted control under the same input. Do not use the result of path normalization to explain the latter.

# Filesystem Mapping Decision Record

This record began with a set of search terms, not a complete implementation description. `filesystem`, `mapper`, `zipfilenamemapper`, `pwd`, and `find_entry` repeatedly led the reading to `lib/zip/filesystem.rb`. The first version therefore made "start reading here" the main direction. That direction is still useful, but its meaning has narrowed: finding a match in an existing rb module establishes only where to start reading, not where the mapper extension is implemented, nor whether extra fields are saved or handed off here.

Three approaches were compared at the time. The first was to continue exploring around the file and record filesystem mapper expansion as a change confined to that file. It took the least time, but tied a path match to implementation ownership. The second was to treat the existing call's retention of local as a complete result. It was more cautious than the first, but a single local result can only show that local remained visible in that call; it cannot serve as evidence for central. The third was to pair a successful call with a failed call and observe local and central extra fields separately. The third approach required more complete samples, but could separate "what the existing call still retained" from "which side disappeared on failure".

| Approach | Basis available at the time | Main issue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expand directly around `lib/zip/filesystem.rb` | File entry point, search terms, existing module | The path cannot establish responsibility for saving fields |
| Use only the local result | The existing call retains local | No corresponding observation for central |
| Compare successful and failed calls | The requirements call for recording results from both sides separately | The original pre-failure input is still missing |

The first approach was later downgraded to a lookup hint. It was not entirely wrong: the earlier investigation did use these terms to reach the file, and continuing to read declarations and their surrounding relationships was still worthwhile. But treating the filename itself as an implementation decision would make it easy to infer, upon later seeing that local remained available, that central was also handled in the same place. No material supported that inference, so it was not retained as a conclusion.

Part of the second approach was retained. local is an identifiable starting point for comparison, and the record should tie it to observations from the specific call rather than adding a generic "the call is normal" at the bottom of the page. central must have its own observation slot. When a result shows only local, central should remain blank; the visibility of local cannot fill in the other side. Even when a successful call produces results on both sides, the record must still preserve which sample each appeared in, rather than compressing them into a single overall label.

The third approach requires the successful and failed samples to have comparable starting points. The successful call provides the baseline: it can tell us whether local or central left visible content in a call. The failed call shows what happened to the same observations on the error path. If the original pre-failure input was not retained, the failure result has no stable reference for comparison; at that point, it is impossible to distinguish a difference in the input itself from one side's fields becoming invisible during processing. This gap is not a blank item in the write-up, but the reason the decision cannot be narrowed further.

## Review Shifted the Focus to Samples

ARC-206 moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-09-30. The following day it moved to Blocked, with the recorded reason being that one original pre-failure input sample was missing. This change over time shifted the question from "which file should we read first" to "does the starting point needed for comparison exist". The file entry point was still valid, but it could no longer explain the blocker; the missing input was the specific reason the review stopped at that time.

This record also provided a counterexample to the early working hypothesis. If the implementation could be inferred solely from the adjacency relationships around `filesystem.rb`, `mapper`, or `find_entry`, the pre-failure input would not have become a blocker. The actual blocker was the prerequisite material for the samples, showing that search hits cannot stand in for field behavior. As a result, the approach of documenting mapper expansion directly under the filename was no longer the primary approach; the file remained an entry point for follow-up review.

ARC-223 concerns a different stage. On 2025-10-30, the testing stage needed someone who could modify fixtures to take over; on 2025-10-31, this card moved to In Progress. The only confirmed point is that adjustments at the fixture entry point were becoming possible. This does not mean that the failed sample has been completed, nor that the central result has passed. Treating "someone can modify the fixtures" and "field behavior has been confirmed" as the same thing would erase the sequence between the two cards.

Accordingly, the review order changed to examine the samples first, then return to the file. First confirm whether the successful and failed calls each have comparable inputs; then record visible results separately for the local and central sides; only then use the declarations and references around `lib/zip/filesystem.rb` to check the scope of mapper code to read. File references can help with navigation, but cannot supply results in place of samples.

## Decisions Made

Keep the existing local call as the baseline, and use paired observations of successful and failed calls. Visible results must be recorded separately for local and central extra fields; when the original pre-failure input is missing, do not infer backward from the failure symptoms that a failure involving the fields has already occurred in the mapper, the saving process, or elsewhere. The current material supports the order of comparison and the boundaries of the record, not new mapper method names, field structures, or call arguments.

Do not use the formulation "a file match establishes implementation ownership". `lib/zip/filesystem.rb` remains the first stop, and while reading, check the declarations and references adjacent to `filesystem`, `mapper`, `zipfilenamemapper`, `pwd`, and `find_entry`; if these names only explain filesystem facade path handling, record only that local relationship, without extending it into ownership of extra fields.

Do not use the "track only local" formulation. That the existing call retains local is a fact worth keeping, but its scope ends there. When central has no observation of its own, the conclusion should explicitly stop at local; the normal behavior of a successful sample cannot explain the cause for a failed sample, nor can a successful sample fill the gaps in a failed one.

Do not wait for every question to have an answer before keeping a record, either. Why the first draft began with the mapper file, why ARC-206 was blocked by missing input, and why ARC-223 addressed fixtures first are all necessary parts of how the decision took shape. Deleting them would leave later readers with a rule that has no provenance, and obscure the point at which the early judgment was narrowed.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> LocalBaseline
    LocalBaseline: Retain the existing local call
    LocalBaseline --> PairedReview
    PairedReview: Observe successful and failed calls separately
    PairedReview --> MissingInput
    MissingInput: Original pre-failure input is missing
    MissingInput --> FixtureWork
    FixtureWork: Continue preparation once fixtures can be modified
    FixtureWork --> PendingComparison
    PendingComparison: central result pending confirmation
```

The states in the diagram indicate only how this decision is constrained by the material. Start with the local baseline, then require the two types of calls to be paired; when input is missing, comparison stops at the missing sample; once fixtures can be modified, preparation can continue, but that does not justify declaring that a central result has been obtained. The endpoint remains pending comparison so that the start of work on ARC-223 is not misrepresented as a conclusion about field behavior.

## Keep the Two Types of Records Separate

A successful sample should preserve the local and central results actually visible in one call. Here, "successful" describes only the sample path; it does not mean that filesystem mapper expansion is complete. A failed sample should preserve both the input from before the failure and the visible results after it. If the former is missing, the latter, even if present, can only be recorded as an observation without the prerequisites for comparison.

If the successful sample retains only local, the record should state that local is visible and central is unconfirmed; if only one side is still visible after the failed sample has been completed, the gaps should likewise be preserved according to the actual observations. The two calls cannot be merged into the same state just because both mention extra fields. There are four positions to compare: local in the successful call, central in the successful call, local in the failed call, and central in the failed call.

Nor does a field being "visible" here mean that the field has been fully saved at some layer. It only indicates that the result left identifiable content at the point of observation for that call. Handoffs between the mapper, filesystem facade, or other adjacent declarations must be supported jointly by subsequent actual references and samples. The current path material has only navigational value and does not provide enough implementation detail to fill in the gaps.

## File Entry Point and Related Records

Follow-up review starts at `lib/zip/filesystem.rb` because the terms used in the earlier investigation did indeed converge here. `pwd` and `find_entry` can narrow the scope of code reading, and `zipfilenamemapper` can preserve clues as to why the earlier investigation used mapper terminology; none of them can establish field behavior based on names alone. If the reading only explains path handling, stop at that local declaration rather than extending the call name into responsibility for fields.

DOC-16 concerns iterator close lifecycle and central IO entry count. It and this page both mention central, but refer to different objects. This page does not borrow from DOC-16 to fill in conclusions about extra fields, nor does it extend this page's requirements for successful and failed samples to entry count. The two records can point to each other, but cannot substitute for each other.

ARC-206 continues to correspond to the blocker caused by missing pre-failure input; ARC-223 corresponds to the start of work once fixtures could be modified. Their roles differ: the former explains why the comparison remains incomplete, while the latter explains which preparation conditions changed. Together, they do not establish that processing of central is complete.

## Retained Items

"filesystem mapper expansion mainly falls around `filesystem.rb`" is retained as an early working hypothesis, no longer as an implementation decision. It explains the original reading route, but does not stand up to scrutiny when a path match is equated directly with field ownership. The fact that the existing call retains local still holds, but only as a local baseline; central still needs to be observed separately in the successful and failed samples.

Next time material is added, first preserve the original pre-failure input, then record the local and central results from the two types of calls side by side. Adding only file references can narrow the reading scope, but cannot complete the field comparison; adding only an entry point for modifying fixtures can advance sample preparation, but cannot replace the pre-failure input. Once the material is available, decide whether there is a more direct relationship between the mapper entry point and the field results.

# Iterator Close and Entry Count Proposal

Start the review by separating two adjacent observations that should not be conflated: `iterator close lifecycle` focuses on who owns the close operation when the iterator ends, while `central IO entry count` focuses on how many times the shared entry point is traversed during a single read. The earlier investigation put filesystem, iterator, close, tell, read, and rewind on the same search path, making it easy to mistake call adjacency for ownership. Leave this question open here; do not treat the path location of `lib/zip/filesystem.rb` directly as an interface decision.

Option A makes a local record of the order of iterator entry, return, and close. It is closest to the lifecycle issue: it shows whether close occurs after the first result is returned and preserves the order between read and rewind; the trade-off is that, if another entry point handles the close operation, the local record may not capture the full chain. Option B records only the central IO entry count and compares it with the actual file IO entry count. It makes it easier to detect repeated entry or cases where the expected entry was not traversed, but the number alone cannot show which call owns the closing responsibility.

At the time, the inclination was to try A first, then use B for a cross-check. Limit the check to filesystem-related adjacencies in the current revision: first select a path capable of returning an iterator result, and record the order of entry, read, rewind, and close; then record the central IO entry count for the same usage pattern. If the two observations conflict, retain the raw records first; do not interpret count as meaning that close has completed. The counterexample here is that the read operation has already returned, but the iterator close still has not been observed on the same path; this only indicates that the observation scope is insufficient and cannot directly establish an implementation leak.

The trade-off is the size of the change. Moving close to obtain a count would change the lifecycle under review; merging entry points to make the count look better would mask repeated reads. Therefore, the first round will not change the interface, turn the file IO entry count into a new public convention, or replace the existing return behavior. If a comparison is needed, use two records from the same read path to avoid combining numbers from different usage patterns into a single conclusion.

The withdrawal criteria are simple: if the local record requires changing the close order, or the central IO entry count cannot be matched to a specific read action, drop the experimental record, leaving existing behavior and open questions. Only if A and B can both be matched consistently should we move to the next interface discussion. What remains undecided is whether the responsibility boundary for close should be written into the iterator entry, and whether the count should belong to central IO or file IO; do not decide either of these on this page prematurely.

# Entry Lifecycle Decision Record

The initial draft placed reset defaults, Zip64 mode, and entry dirty lifecycle under `Zip::Entry`. This came from the names and file entry points carried over from earlier calls, not from having already identified a state chain shared by all three. Old links still lead people here, so the initial draft was not deleted; but continuing to read it as implementation ownership would incorrectly turn "appeared in the same round" into "written in the same place."

This page preserves the trade-offs made at the time. It is not responsible for restating the Dirtyable setter contract for DOC-21, nor does it turn Zip64 record boundaries into documentation for Entry's fields. The Entry file is simply a local place where this group of issues can converge: the module is on line 2, and the class is on line 3; default variables, name checks, initialization, time reads, and file-type checks can all be found in this object.

## The Initial Draft's Combined Framing

The earlier calls were concerned with the results left after reset defaults. Meanwhile, Zip64 mode came up in the investigation, and another entry point was reported as entry dirty lifecycle. The initial judgment was practical but rough: do not change the handling of default variables just to trace mode; and do not assume that the entry's subsequent modification state is no longer a problem simply because the object can be initialized.

At the time, the three names were grouped mainly to prevent two opposing kinds of changes. One approach treated the default state as an irrelevant detail and pursued a new path focused only on mode; the other preserved the defaults but failed to ask how an Entry is treated after it is modified. Either could cause the results of the earlier calls to disappear, but at the time this risk could not yet be tied to a particular member or write location.

The initial draft's phrasing of "add mode after the defaults" is no longer used. It once constrained the reading scope to an apparently convenient sequence: first find `set_default_vars_values`, then assume that the Zip64 issues would be filled in afterward. The available code-location material gives no such sequence, nor does it show mode being set by that method. That passage remains in the historical version to explain why old links point to Entry; it cannot serve as an order for making changes.

Likewise, the early term "full reset" should remain in its old context. All that can be confirmed here is that the declaration `set_default_vars_values` exists; this does not establish that it covers every member, that it goes through every reconstruction path, or, still less, that it affects content already written out. Calling it a full reset would lead later readers to mistakenly believe that the defaults issue already has a fully defined scope.

## File-Level Adjacencies Seen in This Review

`lib/zip/entry.rb` remains the only stable code location for this page. The directly locatable snippets are as follows:

```ruby
module Zip
  class Entry
    def set_default_vars_values
    def check_name(name)
    def initialize
    def time
    def file_type_is
```

These names show that default variables, name checks, object initialization, time reads, and type checks exist side by side locally within Entry. They do not automatically form a call sequence. In particular, the material reaches no conclusion about the actual relationship between `check_name(name)` and dirty lifecycle; this record also does not confirm whether `time` and `file_type_is` are query-only.

Their coexistence in the file is still useful when reading the code. When modifying `initialize`, default-variable initialization must not be treated as an unrelated side issue; when looking at name checks, the entry's visible-state issues should not be attributed directly to its name either. This reminder is much weaker than "they share a lifecycle," but it is closer to the available facts.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Zip::Entry" as Entry
  state "set_default_vars_values" as Defaults
  state "check_name(name)" as NameCheck
  state "initialize" as Initialize
  state "time" as Time
  state "file_type_is" as FileType
  [*] --> Entry
  Entry --> Defaults : locate
  Entry --> NameCheck : locate
  Entry --> Initialize : locate
  Entry --> Time : locate
  Entry --> FileType : locate
```

The diagram shows only lookup relationships within the file; its arrows are not state transitions. Previously, someone followed the method names and connected default variables, mode, and dirty marker into a single flow; that is precisely the reading being retracted in this round.

## Decisions Retained

Decision 1: Continue keeping reset defaults and Zip64 mode in the same historical record, but no longer describe them as a single implementation point. Keeping them on the same page is not a technical merger; it reflects the fact that the earlier calls and old investigation names still lead back to Entry together. If they were immediately split into two short pages with no explanation of their relationship, readers coming through the old entry points might still merge them again, only without this correction.

Decision 2: Changes involving `set_default_vars_values` or `initialize` must not use "the object can still be created" as a substitute for reviewing the earlier results for the defaults. This review concerns the reset defaults results left by the earlier calls, not a set of fields newly defined on this page. This scope has deliberately not been expanded, because the record does not preserve the complete process of replaying the calls.

Decision 3: Keep Zip64 mode as an item to check in the same batch, not as a description of `set_default_vars_values`'s responsibilities. When someone needs to determine Zip64 record boundaries or where mode takes effect, they should continue tracing from actual references; the name defaults alone is not enough to decide how Entry's default state should change.

Decision 4: Retain entry dirty lifecycle separately as a user entry point adjacent to Entry. Passing the defaults checks does not also justify declaring dirty lifecycle covered; conversely, dirty-related behavior does not invalidate the reset defaults results that the earlier calls depend on. The evidence for the two differs in strength in this material: the former is backed by the context of earlier calls, while the latter has only a description of the user-visible entry point.

The proposed reorganization of "first perform a unified reset, then fill in state according to Zip64 mode" was not adopted here. On the surface, it could arrange the three issues into a clear sequence of steps, but the source-file locations do not support that sequence. Writing this assumption into the decision record would encourage later contributors to add state at the wrong level, so it has been explicitly discontinued.

## The Division of Work Later Established by the Cards

ARC-211 records that the earlier calls preserve the reset defaults results, and keeps reset defaults and Zip64 mode as routine maintenance checks. It explains why defaults and mode appear side by side on this old page, but does not bind them into the responsibility of a single method.

ARC-228 starts from entry dirty lifecycle and calls for recovering the most recent actual call and the result seen by the user. It adds call-side information, not a definition of default variables. If all that is available is new names, screenshots, or summaries, that is still not enough to fill in the location of dirty marker; this page should not rewrite the pending investigation items in ARC-228 as completed implementation documentation either.

Once follow-up work began, the two cards took on different roles: ARC-211 preserves the default results of the earlier calls, while ARC-228 fills in what actually happened at the user entry point. Keeping them side by side is intended to let readers arriving through Entry know that the issues were once mixed together; their placement side by side should no longer be taken to imply the same priority.

## Items Still in the Margins

Whether `check_name(name)` has any actual connection to dirty lifecycle has not yet been established. Nor has it been recorded whether `time` and `file_type_is` are merely similar query methods within this group of issues. They remain listed here only because they are all in the same Entry file and provide useful stopping points when reading; this does not mean a connection to Zip64 or the defaults has been confirmed.

The purpose of this record is now narrower than that of the initial draft: it preserves the old grouping and the subsequent decision to split it. Defaults must not be casually erased in the course of addressing mode; the implementation boundaries of mode cannot be inferred from the name defaults; and the dirty lifecycle still needs actual calls before there is enough material to close it out. The old investigation entry points remain usable, but the old framing itself should not be extended further.

# Entry Timestamps and Dirty Flags Proposal

FAT timestamp restoration and the Dirtyable setter contract were initially included in the same interface review because both involve the state of `Zip::Entry`. This was only a working hypothesis: appearing on the same object does not mean they should be handled by the same method, the same initialization logic, or the same writeback.

For now, use `lib/zip/entry.rb` as a starting point for reading. From there, you can locate `module Zip`, `class Entry`, as well as `set_default_vars_values`, `check_name(name)`, `initialize`, `time`, and `file_type_is`. Of these, `time` is worth tracing back through its callers; default-value initialization should also be checked, but that alone is not grounds for treating all setters as the same kind of change.

The proposal is to start with two independent records:

- Timestamp restoration: start from where `time` is read and used, and identify what state is retained before and after the restoration operation enters `Entry`.
- Dirty flags: confirm at the actual setter entry points which assignments change an entry's commit state and which are only assignments during construction or validation.
- Discuss the two records together only if they can be tied to the same state transition.

We are not committing to any new interfaces in this round. We need one restoration path and one setter path first, before deciding whether callers expect a return status or object state, or whether neither should be exposed.

# Proposal for Entry Timestamps and Dirty Marking

The original proposal to combine the work is retained here, not because it is now a settled conclusion, but because later discussions can easily turn "both are near Entry" into "both must be changed together". The user-visible effects of both issues occur during the archive entry lifecycle, but one concerns whether FAT timestamp restoration can be reflected in the appropriate timestamp interface, while the other concerns whether the Dirtyable setter contract leaves changes that can be committed after an assignment. They can share a starting point for reading the code, but we cannot assume a single implementation conclusion for both.

## Assessments from the Initial Draft

The initial draft used `lib/zip/entry.rb` as the starting point for verification and suggested tracing time and assignments separately. At that point, it also tended to view default-value initialization as the common center of both issues: if state is established in `set_default_vars_values`, perhaps both restoration and dirty marking could be explained from there.

That inference has now been narrowed. Initialization is indeed a place we should read, but it only tells us that `Entry` contains code that sets default values. It does not prove that restoration happens there, nor does it prove that every setter should produce a dirty marker. Continuing to treat this inference as a design premise would lead the subsequent implementation to fill two unverified gaps with one sweeping change.

## What the Review Can Confirm

The identifiable objects in the current file remain limited: `module Zip` contains `class Entry`; the class contains `set_default_vars_values`, `check_name(name)`, `initialize`, `time`, and `file_type_is`. This is enough to prioritize the code reading, and enough to rule out an unsound claim: we cannot assert that timestamp restoration is the exclusive responsibility of `Entry` merely because `time` is adjacent to the initialization method; nor can we expand Dirtyable's scope to all field writes merely because we see default values.

`check_name(name)` and `file_type_is` should also remain in view. The former reminds us that validation-related assignments may occur during construction; the latter reminds us that not all entry attributes are equivalent to content modifications. These are only branches to follow while reading, however, not conclusions about their internal behavior. The locations identified so far do not establish FAT encoding or platform time semantics, nor do they provide a list of setters or the storage location of the dirty state.

## Revised Trial Plan

This time, we do not recommend first designing a new interface that covers both issues. Start by documenting two minimal paths, and make each record independently falsifiable by counterexamples.

**Timestamp restoration path.** Trace backward from the locations that call `time`: does the caller receive a restored time, a raw time, or a value that still needs interpretation; then check whether there is already an identifiable metadata handoff before that value enters `Entry`. If restoration occurs before object creation, then `Entry` only needs to preserve its existing read interface; only if restoration must depend on state inside the entry should we discuss what information to retain at the object boundary. The candidate here is not "always restore during initialization", but "let the actual data handoff determine the restoration point".

**setter path.** Start from the entry points that actually write to the entry, and distinguish assignments during construction, assignments during validation, and deliberate modifications by callers. Option one is for all externally exposed setters to leave a dirty marker. Its advantage is a simple mental model for callers, but its cost is that default values and derived properties may be incorrectly reported as pending commit. Option two is to mark only assignments already proven to affect archive output. Its cost is that the boundaries must be explained item by item, and missing even one genuine modification would make the example and the commit state inconsistent. For now, option two is better treated as a direction for investigation rather than immediately declared a rule; the reason is not that it is more conservative, but that the available material does not yet provide the complete set of setters.

The two paths share just one requirement: the records should clearly state where state changes, where callers observe the changes, and what the counterexamples are. The timestamp path must not substitute "the object has been initialized" for evidence of restoration; the setter path must not substitute "the field looks important" for evidence of a commit. This will allow later reviews to compare the compatibility costs of the two options rather than compare two naming schemes.

## Why Not Combine the Implementations

Binding timestamp restoration to dirty marking may appear to eliminate one state-handling step, but in practice it would stack two risks together. If timestamp restoration is a read-side interpretation, it should not trigger commit state without reason; if a setter merely performs an internal assignment during construction or validation, it should not be used to prove that the FAT timestamp has been restored. Only when the path records show that the same write both changes the data on which restoration depends and actually changes archive output is there a reason to discuss a shared state transition.

Therefore, reviews should prioritize comparing two types of cost: whether the timestamp interface of `Entry` can still meet callers' needs when restoration logic is outside the object boundary; and whether narrowing dirty marking to actual output changes misses any existing modification entry points. In the former case, do not stuff restoration state into `Entry` without evidence, and in the latter, do not elevate default assignments to externally visible modifications without evidence.

## Withdrawal and Open Items

If the timestamp path cannot identify a clear point where restoration data enters the object, withdraw any proposal requiring `Entry` to take on new restoration responsibilities; if the setter path cannot distinguish writes during construction from caller modifications, withdraw the proposal to "mark all setters uniformly". Until both investigations are complete, do not treat the same dirty marker as a substitute signal for successful timestamp restoration.

Only a few specific questions remain to be answered: where callers of `time` obtain its value; whether the data needed for restoration has already been handed off before the entry is created; which actual setters affect archive output; and which layer ultimately reads Dirtyable's marker. Once these paths are available, decide whether the interface needs to change or whether only a more narrowly scoped calling convention needs to be added.

# Central Parsing and Commit-Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

Record the troubleshooting entry point first in `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`. Older records may end up here because of terms such as `central`, `directory`, `record`, and `entry`, but a path match can only serve as a starting point for back-checking; the filename alone cannot establish central parser ownership.

## First classify the anomaly

```text
central record / entry read anomaly
├─ Can the corresponding read, traversal, or result handoff be seen in the file?
│  ├─ Yes: note the adjacent method name, then verify references
│  └─ No: stop at the file entry; add the record declaration or call name
├─ Abnormal state after archive commit?
│  ├─ Observations from before and after commit available: record state and output separately
│  └─ Only a single symptom: fill in the original state first; do not replay directly
└─ Occurs only on a particular path?
   ├─ Path can be retained: note the directory or file boundary
   └─ Boundary unclear: retain the original path; stop assigning cause
```

### central branch

Once the actual read operation is found, record the input object, output object, and next hop. If there is only a search hit, write "File entry found; references not verified"; do not treat the existence of an entry as confirmation of parser ownership.

### commit branch

Record separately the pre-commit state, post-commit state, whether output already exists, and the path associated with the output. Output having been produced does not mean the state check is complete; a state change does not mean the write has completed. If the four items cannot be aligned, retain the original record and do not change the restoration logic yet.

### path branch

Retain the original path used by the triggering operation, and distinguish between directory and file. If only the path name is visible and the boundary cannot be determined, save the path observation separately. A path boundary cannot establish where the central parser is implemented, and the post-commit state cannot replace path verification.

One incident can enter multiple branches at the same time, but write them as a single record only when the read action, state change, and path boundary can all be aligned in time. Otherwise, retain the gaps separately.

# Central Parsing and Commit Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

This page covers three observations that often appear next to one another in the same on-call log but are not interchangeable: reads of a central record or entry, the state before and after an archive commit, and the path passed with the triggering operation. Enter the tree based on the object observed during the incident, rather than inferring ownership from the filename.

The easiest entry point to find in searches is still `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`. The repository index lists it as an existing rb module, making it useful for code reading and checking historical behavior. The terms `central`, `directory`, `record`, `entry` can help locate it, but a keyword match, a file path match, and an actual reference are three different things. To attribute the issue to central parser ownership, you must at least be able to identify an actual read or traversal operation in the file and explain where its result is handed off; if all you see is a declaration or search results, stop the investigation at the entry point.

## Local Facts Recorded at the Start of the On-Call Shift

Do not replay the commit yet, and do not start by writing that central parsing failed. Break the original log down into the following items, preserving the order in which they actually appeared during the incident:

- Whether the triggering action was reading a central record, processing an entry, executing an archive commit, or accessing a path;
- Whether the observed object was a central record, an entry, the archive state, output, or the original path;
- Whether the observation occurred before an action, after an action, or between two actions;
- Whether `lib/zip/central_directory.rb` was found through an actual declaration, an adjacent call, or only a keyword search;
- Whether there are state records both before and after the commit, and whether output has already been produced;
- Whether the path is still preserved as-is, and whether directory boundaries and file boundaries can be distinguished.

If the last item contains only a cleaned-up path and not the original path passed in when the operation was triggered, first write "original path missing". Do not substitute a normalized path for the input. If you find only the file without seeing any calls, retain the file entry point and do not fill in a seemingly complete ownership conclusion.

## Which Tree to Follow First

```text
Encountering an exception related to central / commit / path
├─ 1. Initial incident evidence points to a central record or entry
│  ├─ A read, traversal or result handoff is visible
│  │  └─ Record the objects and adjacent methods, and verify them by following one-hop references
│  ├─ Only declarations or search hits are visible
│  │  └─ Stop at the file entry point, and obtain the call name or record source
│  └─ The read and commit are only adjacent in time
│     └─ First record them as two separate entries, and do not treat their sequence as a handoff
├─ 2. Initial incident evidence points to the state after archive commit
│  ├─ State observations are available both before and after commit
│  │  └─ Verify the state transition, output and path objects separately
│  ├─ Only a state change is visible
│  │  └─ Mark the output as unconfirmed, and do not describe the state change as a successful commit
│  ├─ Only output generation is visible
│  │  └─ Recheck the state and path, as output alone is not enough to close the investigation
│  └─ The before-and-after observations cannot be ordered
│     └─ Stop recovery actions, and preserve the original chronological order
└─ 3. The issue occurs only with a particular path or path form
   ├─ The original path is clearly a directory
   │  └─ Record the directory boundary separately, then check whether the exception occurs before or after access
   ├─ The original path is clearly a file
   │  └─ Keep the file object, output object and archive state separate
   ├─ The original path is preserved but its boundary is unclear
   │  └─ Compare only the path observations, without deciding whether it is a directory or a file
   └─ The original path was not retained
      └─ Stop at the path branch, and first obtain the triggering input
```

The three entry points in the tree can occur at the same time. For example a commit may occur immediately after a central record is read, or a path may then be accessed after commit. Temporal proximity only shows that they occur in the same incident context, not that the state was produced by the same piece of code. Only when the observation points, objects and sequence for each can all be aligned, should you proceed to cross-checking.

## A: central record / entry

Use `lib/zip/central_directory.rb` to find the relationships among central, record and entry that actually appear in the file. After finding a loop, a read or a result handoff, follow references one hop outward, first record the direct neighbors, and do not copy the entire ArchiveKit call chain. The minimum required record is: the object obtained before the action, the object produced by the action, the next visible call name, and when the exception appears.

### A specific read operation is visible

Document the input and output separately. The input may be a central record or the entry being traversed; the output should be the object actually observed in the incident context, without using one generic term for both. If the result was saved, but no subsequent use was observed, note "Result handoff not checked further". This indicates the stopping point reached in the current investigation, not that there is no code afterward.

If you can see an entry but have not matched it to the source of the central record, first trace back to the source. The presence of an entry only shows that an entry observation point has appeared, and does not mean that the central parser has completed all its work. Conversely, if you only see central-related names without any read operations, do not attribute all central issues to this file either.

### Keyword hits only

Keep filenames and search terms as navigation information. At this point, there are only two actions you can take next: confirm whether the file contains the corresponding declaration, or supply the actual call name. Without these two items, do not continue inferring ownership along the tree, and do not record a path hit as a result handoff. If an adjacent call is found later, record the discovery order again; a new adjacency observation must not be backfilled as having been confirmed from the start.

### central and commit appear together

Make a local record with two columns: in the left column, record the actions and objects for central record / entry, and in the right column, record the state, output, and paths before and after archive commit. Only put them into a single review record when both columns can point to the same object or a clear handoff point. If they can only be linked by their temporal order, keep them separate. This avoids treating a read anomaly directly as the cause of commit.

### Stop conditions for branch A

In all of the following cases, stop at the central branch: only the path for `lib/zip/central_directory.rb` is found; only search results for `central` or `record` are found; an entry is seen but has no source; a result is seen being saved but there is no next hop; the read time and commit time cannot be ordered. When stopping, retain the objects and original descriptions already observed, and do not infer the parser's scope of responsibility from the gaps.

## B: archive commit

"Abnormal state after commit" is only the symptom that leads into branch B. First confirm what object was saved before commit, what state was observed after commit returned, whether output has already been produced, and whether the path object still matches the triggering input. Record state values, output, and path names separately, without treating path names as state values or output files as state updates.

### Two sets of observations before and after commit are available

Split them into two sets by time, rather than compressing both sets into a single result statement:

```text
Before commit: object / state / original path
commit action: action actually observed on site
After commit: object / state / output / path
```

If the same object can be located both before and after, continue checking whether the state is empty, has changed, or was not observed. If the objects before and after are different, first record the object change, and do not assume it is a state transition for the same commit. If the path was replaced between the two sets, record only the fact of the replacement, and do not interpret it as a result of commit for now.

### Output has already been produced

The fact that output has already been produced only indicates that a write operation met the observation conditions in the actual environment. It cannot replace verification of the archive state, nor can it prove that the path used for the output is the path in the triggering input. Continue checking each item separately: whether the state before commit was retained, whether the state after commit was retained, whether the output and path can be matched to each other, and whether the central record was read before or after commit.

If any of the four items is missing, retain the output already produced, and do not delete it and retry as the first step. Deleting or rewriting will erase the evidence needed to distinguish the state, output, and path. Missing items should be written directly in the record, for example "output observed, state after commit not observed" or "state changed, output path not aligned", rather than reframing the gap as an explanation of failure.

### Only a state change is observed

A state change does not mean commit succeeded. First write "output not confirmed", then check whether the original input can still be obtained. If the input has not changed, you can use the same input for one read-only check; if the input has changed, record the change itself, and do not treat the second observation as the result of the first commit. Without the input, output, and order of events, do not perform recovery actions that would rewrite the archive.

### Only a statement that an anomaly occurred after commit

Return to the object and path from before commit. Without the state before commit, you cannot determine where the change began; without an output record, you cannot determine whether a write occurred; without the original path, you cannot determine whether the path branch was involved. At this point, stop the investigation at filling in the missing records in branch B, rather than directly replaying the commit. If a replay has already occurred, it must be listed separately as a new observation, with a note that it occurred after the original observation.

### Before and after cannot be aligned

A common source of confusion is putting the archive state before the operation started, the object state after the operation returned, and subsequent path access on the same line. When you encounter this kind of record, split it into three parts in order of occurrence. If the order cannot be determined, retain "order undetermined", and stop recovery writes. The only follow-up needed is to add the order, the object being observed, and the output, with no need to provide an attribution first.

## C: path boundary

Branch C handles only path boundaries. First retain the original path passed to the triggering operation exactly as supplied, then mark whether the actual observations show a directory boundary, a file boundary, or no way to distinguish between them. The path branch does not prove where the central parser is implemented, nor does it prove that archive commit has completed.

### Directory boundary

If the original path is clearly a directory, first check whether the anomaly had already appeared before crossing the directory boundary. If a central record or entry anomaly had already been observed before then, the directory is only an adjacent observation; if there was no anomaly before then, record the state after directory access. Successful directory access cannot replace verification of the commit state, and the directory name cannot replace the original path.

If the determination of the directory boundary comes from a processed path, rather than the triggering input, retain "boundary determination is based on processed results". Do not upgrade this to a confirmed directory input. Only take the directory branch in the tree when the actual observations themselves allow the distinction to be made.

### File boundary

Record the file path separately from the output object. The file object existing, the output having been generated, and the archive state having been updated are three different observations. If any one is missing, you can stop at the missing item, without using the filename to infer the state. If the file path differs from the output path, first retain both paths; whether they should be the same is a matter for a later check, and no conclusion should be drawn directly in this branch.

### Boundary Undetermined

This is a valid stopping point. Preserve the original path, trigger action, and last known object, and wait for input that can distinguish a directory from a file. If only one path string remains, do not choose one interpretation just to let the tree continue downward, and do not pass off the normalized path result as the trigger input. At this point, do not change the parser's determination, and do not infer the path boundary backward from the state after commit.

### Path Intersecting with the Other Two Branches

When the path is clear but there is no observation from the central read, limit the conclusion to the path evidence. When the central read is clear but the path boundary is undetermined, limit the conclusion to the central observation. When the states before and after commit are clear but the path is missing, limit the conclusion to the state observation. Only when all three can be aligned should the object, order, and direct adjacency be placed in the same review record. Each record retains its own stopping reason; a confirmed fact in one cannot be used to fill a gap in either of the other two.

## Actual Order of the Cross-Check

When the evidence mentions central parser, archive commit, and path boundary at the same time, start with the trigger input, not the filename:

```text
Original trigger input
  └─ Is the original path still present?
       ├─ No: stop at missing path input
       └─ Yes
          └─ Is the directory or file boundary clear?
               ├─ No: stop at path boundary
               └─ Yes
                  └─ Is there an actual read observation for the central record / entry?
                       ├─ No: retain the file entry point and stop at the central branch
                       └─ Yes
                          └─ Are there state observations both before and after commit?
                               ├─ No: retain the existing observations; do not perform recovery writes
                               └─ Yes: then recheck the output, path, and direct handoff points
```

This sequence serves one purpose: first ensure that the trigger input has not been replaced by the process of organizing the evidence, then determine the path boundary, and only afterward inspect reads and state. It does not require every case to reach the end. If a case stops at missing path input, there is no need to add nonexistent input just to find the central entry point; if a case stops at the file entry point, there is likewise no need to fill commit state into the central branch.

If the central read, commit, and path observations come from different points in time, retain the time points separately. An object absent from the previous record cannot be backfilled into that record just because it appears in a later record. What can be confirmed is "an object was seen later"; what cannot be confirmed is that it participated in the same action from the beginning.

## When Replay Has Already Been Performed

Earlier troubleshooting involved three actions that could easily disturb the original evidence: immediately replaying after seeing an anomaly after commit, attributing the central parser to a file upon seeing its filename, and assuming a path is a directory upon seeing it. All of these introduce new actions into subsequent observations.

If a replay has already been performed, save the record in two sections:

```text
Original observations: triggering input / original path / known states before and after commit / existing output
Subsequent observations: objects, states, output, and paths seen after the replay action
```

Replay results can only serve as new observations; they cannot be used to backfill the original states before and after commit. If there was no input or output before the replay, explicitly state that the original evidence lacks that item; do not use output that appeared after the replay to backfill what was written the first time. If the replay changed the path or state, retain the change itself, because it explains why the two records cannot be compared directly.

Likewise, actual references found later cannot rewrite earlier search records. If only a file entry point was visible earlier, retain that limitation; when adjacent methods or result handoffs become visible later, append the new verification results. This distinguishes the working hypothesis at the time from subsequent local observations.

## Recording Different Environments

The current material does not include a comparable inventory of runtime environments. If the same phenomenon occurs in different environments, do not explain the differences based on environment names. For each environment, separately record the triggering input, original path, central record / entry observations, state before commit, state after commit, and output status. Only when these fields can be aligned item by item should environment differences be used as a basis for comparison; otherwise, write only "environment differences pending verification" and do not attribute the differences to the parser or path.

If the only information shared across environments is the statement "abnormal state after processing", that statement cannot replace local records. One environment may have output while another has only a state change; one environment may retain the original path while another has only a cleaned-up name. First stop at the missing items in each environment's record, then compare the common fields. Do not invent unobserved values just to produce matching tables.

## Review Record Format

On-call handovers only need to retain the fields needed to return to the original evidence; there is no need to write out the entire call chain:

```text
Trigger: <read / commit / path operation>
Object: <central record / entry / archive state / original path>
Timing: <before the action / after the action / between two actions>
Observation: <what was actually observed>
Entry point: lib/zip/central_directory.rb; <declaration / adjacent method / result handoff / path match only>
Output: <produced / unconfirmed / not observed>
Path boundary: <directory / file / undetermined>
Gap: <specific missing items in the input, output, state, sequence, or references>
```

The content in angle brackets must come from the original evidence. If no output was seen, write "not observed" or "unconfirmed"; do not fill in the result that would usually occur. If no reference was seen, record the path entry point, not a confirmed next hop. When central and commit both appear in a record, the two objects must still be recorded separately; do not retain only a single generic archive state.

If the available evidence is only a one-sentence description, the record may stop at the two lines for the trigger and object. For example, if all that is known is that the state was abnormal after an operation on a path, retain the original path, operation, and abnormal state, and mark the pre-commit state as missing. Do not invent output, parser ownership, or directory boundaries just to make the record look complete.

## Related entry points

ARC-213 is used to check the current entry point and results for central parser. After opening that card, use the minimal directory tree to check whether each candidate path is still reachable; the card previously recorded security triage and changes in the person responsible, but these records do not replace verification of code references.

ARC-230 is used for archive commit state and path boundary. The card's public comments retain this sentence: Suggested next step, on this card ARC-230, there is still one unconfirmed point in archive commit state and path boundary, leave the inputs and outputs from this run in the review thread. This indicates that inputs and outputs are still needed there, so the existence of a card must not be described as verification, nor may the card's records be used to fill in job, commit, or artifact names that are absent from this page.

DOC-23 is an adjacent compatibility-check page. It can be used for navigation, but it does not add any facts about central reads, commit state, or paths on this page. For code entry points, return to `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`, and for event entry points, use ARC-213 or ARC-230, preserving the boundaries of each local issue.

## Where you can stop

- A specific central read or entry handoff has been found, but the reference direction does not fully line up: stop at the entry point within the file, and leave ownership pending verification.
- The pre-commit and post-commit states have been found, but the output or path is missing: stop at the state observation, and do not write it up as a complete commit result.
- The original path and directory or file boundaries have been found, but there is no observation of a central read: stop at the path evidence, and do not attribute the issue to the parser.
- Output is already available but there is no post-commit state: retain the output, add the state, and do not delete or rewrite anything first.
- The commit has already been replayed: keep the post-replay records separate from the original observations, and do not backfill the old state.
- All three can be aligned by the same object and chronological order: only then record their direct adjacency, and place them in the same review record.

When all you can obtain is a statement that the post-processing state is abnormal, stop at the original triggering input, the object being observed, and the gap. File paths, keywords, the card's existence, and a single replay cannot replace separately verifying central record, archive commit, and path boundary.

# Ordinary EOCD field migration notes

"ordinary EOCD fields" was originally just a finding name recorded during pre-release checks. The old records pointed both the issue name and the call name to `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`, so follow-up checks usually started with the central directory file.

The migration approach used at the time was very conservative: leave the finding names in the old records unchanged, and do not replace the file paths; new notes would only append the local objects observed in this pass after the original entry point. This way, the old links could still lead to the material, and renaming would not fold a single anomaly into a broader central directory issue.

The old notes contain an unverified shorthand statement: all state anomalies in ordinary fields can be handled within the central directory. Keep that sentence for now, but do not add a field table or processing order based on it. At the next review, the call name and the objects that actually appear in the file should be recorded separately.

If a new record gets the scope wrong, recover by deleting the added ownership assessment and returning to the old "finding name → central directory file" entry point. The old entry point can only help locate the records from that time.

# Migration notes for ordinary EOCD fields

The old entry point has never been removed. During the release window, people were still searching for "ordinary EOCD fields" and then opening `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`. This entry point came from the investigation notes written at the time, making it easier to find the old issue again; it was later also misused as a complete rule for locating fields.

This review did not rework the field-processing documentation. The focus remains on recording where to start looking, where the old account should stop, and how to preserve the original search terms when returning to old release records.

## The shortcut left by the old records

The earliest version listed only the issue name, call name, and central directory file. It treated the central directory as the first place to check because that was simply where the notes stopped at the time. It did not list the read order for individual ordinary EOCD fields or break out adjacent records separately.

The sentence "If ordinary EOCD fields are abnormal, just check the central directory first" in the old notes was once used as shorthand for release checks. It is retained here so old links and verbal handoffs still line up; it should now be understood as starting from the central directory, not as saying that field processing can occur only there.

This is a small distinction, but it affects how subsequent notes are written. The filename provides an entry point for looking back, and the call name helps locate the old records; neither replaces a review of the objects in the file and the direct references. The old records grouped these things together, making the "first place to check" look like the "processing boundary."

```text
Old release records
  ordinary EOCD fields / Call name
              |
              v
  lib/zip/central_directory.rb
              |
              v
      Local assessment recorded at the time

Review after migration
  Keep the finding name
              |
              v
  central_directory.rb's direct references
          /                 \
         v                   v
  Local relationship seen            Relationship still unclear
  Add to these notes            Keep old entry point and stopping point
```

The lower half of the diagram is a later-added way of recording the review, not a rewrite of the old investigation. The old entry point still serves to retrieve historical material; direct references only limit what can actually be written down in this review. First, keep the finding name unchanged. Do not rename it to "central directory anomaly" or another broad name; otherwise, the old release material will lose its searchable entry point, and the scope will expand into areas that were never confirmed.

Next, open `lib/zip/central_directory.rb` and record the declarations and nearby objects actually seen in this review separately from the old call name. # Sentinel Comment Recovery Decision Record

This record originally treated sentinel comment only as an anomaly that needed to be listed separately. At the time, the risk was not that a definite error had already been found, but that it would be easy to describe "a particular special usage was not recovered" as "archive comments are all unreliable." The two statements would steer follow-up work in different directions: the former requires retaining a set of samples and paths that can be revisited, while the latter would drive broad changes without evidence.

The draft chose to start checking from `lib/zip/central_directory.rb`. This entry has been retained to this day, not because the file path has proved all implementation relationships, but because the name and call clues from the old investigation all converge here. It is suitable as a foothold for reading historical behavior, and for recording a lookup that did not reach the expected branch. It does not automatically mean that this file is responsible for recovery logic, comment-preservation logic, or any other archive lifecycle behavior.

After this review, the issue was narrowed to the following scope:

> For the specific usage of sentinel comment, first confirm whether the central directory side saw and handed off information related to recovery; only after the correspondence between this path and the samples has been recorded should we discuss whether recovery handling needs to change.

Here, sentinel comment refers to an archive comment usage that carries this marker. The current material limits the anomaly to this usage, so ordinary comments, empty comments, and archives in which this marker does not appear should not be casually folded into the same judgment. Keeping the scope narrow does not mean ignoring these cases; it means avoiding replacing the existing issue with counterexamples that have not yet occurred.

## Approaches considered at the time

The first, quicker approach was to infer directly from general comment handling: since an archive comment appeared near the relevant object, assume sentinel was simply a kind of ordinary content and adjust the entire read/write flow first. This was not adopted. This inference skipped sample verification, but rewrote "special usage anomaly" as "ordinary behavior must be anomalous in the same way." If there was no hit, the reader also could not tell whether the sample did not meet the conditions or the recovery path was never reached at all.

The second approach was to treat the path itself as an ownership conclusion: since the investigation clues ultimately pointed to central directory, conclude that all subsequent fixes should stay in that module. This was not adopted either. The path is a useful inspection entry point, but the old record provides navigation, not a complete call attribution. Upgrading navigation to ownership would make later code reading look only for corroboration instead of checking the actual reference relationships.

Another view was to wait until the related issues across the entire archive lifecycle were clarified before recording this point. This direction looked more complete, but in practice it would leave the current anomaly without an actionable foothold. This decision retains a local record: it does not replace the broader lifecycle cleanup, but requires the samples, hits, and misses for sentinel comment to be kept in one place before it is handled. That way, even if it later turns out that the entry needs to move, the original judgment will have a basis that can be revisited.

Therefore, the current decision takes the third approach: use central directory as the starting point and preserve a verification trail for this usage; until the evidence is sufficient to point to the next relationship, do not expand to general comment rules, and do not treat the module location as ownership.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Reported
    Reported --> VerificationEntry: sentinel comment samples
    VerificationEntry --> RetainMiss: Did not enter the target relationship
    VerificationEntry --> RecordHit: Entered recovery verification
    RecordHit --> DetermineNextLocation
    RetainMiss --> AddSampleOrReference
```

The diagram's "determine the next location" is not a specific file designated in advance. It indicates that the hit record gives later work enough information to state: what object was observed, which entry was checked, whether recovery-related information appeared there, and which reference still needs to be followed. If these points are not written down, a standalone "checked" has no value; it can neither explain a miss nor support expanding the processing scope.

## How to write hits and misses

The local requirement for ARC-216 is to leave one hit record and one miss record using the repository's own path-checking method. This does not prescribe any particular command, nor does it replace the execution status recorded on the card; the decision only specifies the distinction that the two records should express.

At a minimum, a hit record should let later people see that the sample really contains the target usage of sentinel comment and that the check reached an entry related to central directory. It does not mean that recovery is already correct, nor that the statement needing modification has been located. If the record only says "saw a comment," it is still impossible to know whether the observation is of the target situation or an ordinary comment.

A miss record likewise cannot be written as "not reproduced." A miss may result from two different situations: the sample did not include the target usage, or the check did not pass through the expected entry. The former means that the sample is unsuitable for answering the current question; the latter means that this choice of entry needs to be traced further along the reference relationships. Neither proves that recovery is error-free, and neither should be used to close ARC-216.

If a single check finds both an ordinary comment and a sentinel comment, they should be written separately in the record. The presence of an ordinary comment only shows that the sample contains a comment; it cannot replace observing the specific usage. Conversely, finding only a sentinel comment without entering the expected entry should not be immediately attributed to central directory; first preserve the reason for the miss, so that the next attempt does not start from the same vague conclusion again.

## Changes from the draft to the review

In the draft, "start from central directory" could easily be read as an implementation assignment. After the review, this entry was retained while two constraints were added: the entry is only for verification; the subsequent location must be determined by the hit record and the reference relationships. This also preserves the draft's practical value—it did provide the first object to inspect—without presenting it as an already-completed technical conclusion.

ARC-216 later first went through an approach comparison and then entered the execution phase. This sequence shows that the issue has moved from mere record-keeping to planned verification, but it cannot be taken to mean that changes have been merged or that any particular recovery behavior has been confirmed. This page does not retain the card's status transitions; it retains only the boundaries that this decision requires to be carried into execution: the sample must represent the target usage; hit and miss records must be separate; the module path cannot replace reference checking.

The related DOC-26 record documents split-module delegation. It can help readers continue looking at the adjacent discussion of the division of responsibilities between modules, but it should not be used to attribute sentinel comment recovery. This decision did not hand the issue over to split-module for handling, nor did it merge their conclusions merely because the two records are adjacent.

## Scope of this decision

This page maintains three local judgments: the anomaly is a specific usage of sentinel comment; `lib/zip/central_directory.rb` is the current first verification entry; without both hit and miss records, the scope of recovery handling should not be expanded.

ARC-216 holds the records of the actual checks. If a hit shows that the entry is merely a handoff point, the card should retain the next reference rather than rewrite the note as "the path assessment was wrong." The path remains a valuable starting point; its meaning has simply become navigation rather than ownership. If the miss comes from the sample conditions, add a sample of the target usage; there is no need to use the opportunity to modify general comment behavior.

The parts still unconfirmed remain open: exactly where in the read stage the recovery action is completed; whether the information seen by central directory is already sufficient to determine recovery; and what content the target sample should retain after passing through this entry. These questions cannot be answered by a filename, the fact that the card entered the execution phase, or a single observation of an ordinary comment. If new reference relationships or sample records emerge later, they should be appended after the corresponding judgment, with an explicit statement of whether they change the entry, the scope, or the recovery conclusion.

Finally, one operational trade-off remains: when there is no target sample, it is preferable to leave a miss marked "sample not applicable" than to package it as a pass. This may make the record appear not to have immediately advanced the fix, but it avoids blurring the boundary of sentinel comment recovery again.
