# Module Delegation Proposal

The early draft began the investigation at `lib/zip/file.rb` and treated "having the split-out modules take over the entry point directly" as a fairly straightforward direction. That assessment remains as historical background and must not be treated as a confirmed implementation relationship: the file location only provides a starting point for checking; it does not establish at which level traversal through the caller's directory begins, or that this file is where it stops.

Later, ARC-217: an additional `caller_walkthrough` called for reproducing split-module delegation from the directory structure supplied by the caller and confirming the actual path where traversal stops. This narrowed the question from "whether the filename is relevant" to a verifiable path record. At a minimum, the walkthrough must record the entry point, the modules traversed, and the stopping point separately; if the directory structure branches along the way, the paths before and after the branch must not be collapsed into a single "file found" conclusion. The card now carries this verification requirement, but this page does not present it as a completed result.

### Options retained from the early draft

**Handoff within the old entry point.**

When existing callers still depend on the old entry point, this option has a smaller migration footprint. Delegation can first be placed near the old entry point, allowing callers to keep using the original location; a full walkthrough can then be observed. The problem is that responsibility will rest with both the old entry point and the split-out modules. If both can be called, subsequent investigation must distinguish between "the old entry point has completed the handoff" and "the new module has become an entry point in its own right"; otherwise, a local success will be mistaken for a fully migrated boundary.

**Direct takeover by the split-out modules.**

This option is only suitable for further comparison if the entry point, the modules traversed, and the stopping point can be reproduced from the directory structure. It can reduce transitional layers, but it brings caller adaptation, path changes, and rollback into the same round of work. The available material does not show that all callers follow the same path, so this remains a candidate, not a decision.

**Transitional entry point.**

A transitional entry point should not be treated as a standalone long-term solution. It is only a migration mechanism, suitable when old calls temporarily cannot be changed but the new modules need to take on some of the relationships first. If used, at a minimum, first clarify what the old entry point accepts, which module it hands off to, and which segment is removed on rollback. If these three points cannot be confirmed, the transitional layer will only stack two unresolved boundaries on top of each other.

### Verification boundaries

Verification should work back from the caller's directory structure to `lib/zip/file.rb`, then check the module declarations and the actual entry relationships. Do not infer delegation simply from similar path names. Only once the walkthrough can reach a stable stopping point can the costs of direct takeover and handoff through the old entry point be compared; if it stops at a gap in the directory structure, the declarations are inconsistent, or the two types of entry points cannot be distinguished, the conclusion remains unconfirmed.

This round must specifically record three migration costs. The first is whether callers must change entry points; the second is the scope in which the old path must remain usable; the third is whether, on failure, delegation can be rolled back without also rolling back caller changes. If reproduction yields no stable stopping point but already requires changes to both the entry point and callers, the candidate changes should be rolled back in this round, the old path retained, and the delegation relationship kept marked as unresolved. The rollback applies only to the experimental delegation; it does not mean deleting this historical record.

### Still undecided after review

- Which side will ultimately own the entry point for the split-out modules;
- Whether to retain the old entry point, and to what extent;
- Whether reproduction from the directory structure yields more than one stopping point;
- Whether caller adaptation can be rolled back independently of delegation.

If verification only confirms the file location, that is still not enough to select an option. Only when a reproducible entry path connects the modules traversed with the stopping point is it worth moving on to the next round of interface review.

# Quality Signal Console Window Checklist

This page was originally a short checklist at the end of the window and still focuses only on borrowing the current entry point, the final output, the return timing, and the rollback entry for adj-zip. It does not cover every test or spec in the quality signal console, nor replace the day-to-day records for regression tiering. The `split archive`, `buffer rewrite` and `metadata handoff` used in the old version remain below for comparison with the state at handoff; these labels are not complete release categories.

## What to leave behind when opening the window

- [ ] Open `docs/adj-zip/release/zip-quality-signal-board-pre-window-close-checklist.md` and confirm that this run continues to use the current entry point, not an old screenshot or bypass name. The entry page is for locating the entry only; store the actual output retained during the window separately beside that run's record.
- [ ] Keep one sample of the project's own success path and one failed sample from a rejection path. Here, a failed sample means a failure already produced by a test or spec that can be attributed, not a conclusion added later.
- [ ] For borrowed content, record the latest return time. If the item to be returned is not clearly specified, do not treat the window as over; retain the final output and entry state first.
- [ ] First check whether the current entry still points to the signal being examined in this window. If the entry has already been redirected, keep the old value as the rollback entry; do not mix the new entry and old output into the same sample.

The old practice was to find `split archive` on the page, preserve the state when `buffer rewrite` appeared, and continue only after `metadata handoff` appeared. That sequence was once short enough, but it conflated "there is a handoff marker" with "the exit action is already consistent." This guidance is still on the page; someone in the window may still use it to find old output.

## Verify item by item before closing the window

1. [ ] Verify the final output itself; do not treat "success" appearing in the logs as a substitute. The output should distinguish the success path for this run, the rejection path, and the failed sample that remains unattributed. If only summary text remains, return to the run record; do not reconstruct the state from memory.
2. [ ] Compare against the regression tiers and keep this run's unstable signal in its original tier. When a single failed sample does not yet establish whether it was caused by a test, a spec, or a change to the entry point, mark it as unattributed; do not move it into the stable tier just to close the window.
3. [ ] Remove the temporary bypass kept for this window, then check whether the entry still receives new work. If the output continues to change after the bypass is removed, stop cleaning up and retain the rollback entry and the last outputs from before and after the change.
4. [ ] Return the borrowed content. If the order of the return action and the final output cannot be confirmed, roll back using the old entry; do not treat "already looked at it once" as completion of the return.
5. [ ] Do not fold incomplete items into "the project team will continue to monitor." If the path branches after the current entry, route the branch to the current maintainer; this is also the reason for the maintainer reassignment recorded in ARCA-017.

The records for ARCA-004 previously called out a case that the old checklist did not break out: the rollback state and the exit action may not match. This cannot be used to record any partial recovery as fully complete. If the rollback entry is available but the exit action still does not line up, stop the window at the rollback entry and retain the original failed sample. ARCA-004 was later blocked for a time because the caller-provided failed sample was still missing; therefore, when no failed sample is available, the check before closing the window records only the gap and does not attribute the signal to the caller.

## Stop and roll back

Stop if any of the following occurs: `metadata handoff` does not appear; the final output cannot be matched to the current entry; the borrowed content has no return time; or the entry still receives new work after rollback. Stopping does not mean deleting actions already taken. Keep the current entry, final output, and rollback entry; the next window continues from here.

The rollback order remains as described on the old page: restore the old value first, then remove the temporary bypass, then handle the return. This order does not prove that all exit actions are consistent; it was simply the conservative practice left at the time. ARCA-030 note that version synchronization for adj-zip may lag, so the old value cannot be discarded immediately when closing the window.

## Old notes left on the page

"Do not clear the run state after seeing `buffer rewrite`" remains valid, but the checks that followed it used to be compressed into a single `metadata handoff`, making it easy to overlook the failed sample and the return timing. People who have not updated this short checklist may still mistake the handoff marker for the end marker.

ARCA-004, ARCA-017, and ARCA-030 can be used to find the respective rollback, maintainer, and version-synchronization records; this page keeps only the stop points for this window.

# Signal Dashboard Cache Trade-off Record

This discussion kept two questions separate: whether `extra field` should stay on the existing path, and whether `compression registry` should be split out on its own. The former involves fewer changes and lets us keep using the existing pages and cache; the latter would separate compression-related records from the present structure, but would mean entry-point changes and caller updates. The disagreement was not about naming, but about the different states the two options would leave behind on failure.

When we reviewed the existing material, the two failure-exit sections in `docs/adj-zip/decisions/zip-quality-signal-cache-vs-original-environment-tradeoffs.md` did not point to the same location. Rebuilding the environment outright would let the results from a clean environment mask the original state this failure depended on, making it hard to tell later whether differences came from the revision, cache, or structural split. There was also an objection that keeping the old environment would carry past problems forward, especially since the active callers of `compatibility check` had not yet been fully verified. That objection is retained in the record without treating conjecture as a verified conclusion.

The decision in this version is to keep the current revision for now and not rebuild the environment. This preserves the existing runtime state; it does not confirm that the state is suitable for long-term use. When comparing `extra field` and `compression registry`, do not introduce an environment rebuild as a third variable; if a rerun is needed, keep `zip-quality-signal`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and change only the revision. The resulting differences can still be traced back to the same runtime state, at least avoiding mistaking environment changes for implementation changes.

At the time, there was still a preference for splitting `compression registry` out on its own, because its failure exits would be easier to observe in isolation and compression signals would no longer need to be crammed into `extra field`. But this was only a preferred direction, not a finalized migration decision. `compatibility check` had not confirmed the callers, and whether rollback should restore only the old entry point was also undecided, so these two items cannot be listed as pass criteria.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Stall Troubleshooting Tree

When the current entry point stalls, first check whether what remains is a captured failure state or a page already overwritten by a later rerun. For the former, you can continue from the record; for the latter, you can only start by retrieving the earliest record. Don't infer what happened in between from the final display, directory names, or a green status in a screenshot.

```text
Does the current entry point have an original record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Screenshot only: keep the screenshot and obtain the original request or original record
│  └─ Not even a screenshot: log the gap and stop root-cause analysis
└─ Yes
   ├─ The record still points to zip-quality-signal: run an in-project comparison
   ├─ The record shows an exit action: first identify the original request for that action
   └─ Required records are inaccessible due to permissions: hand off to the permissions owner
```

The original record is more than the last line displayed on the page. Whoever takes over must at least be able to identify the current entry point, the first result observed, the command used, and the current revision. If any item is missing, note it alongside the captured state; don't fill the gap with a later run and call it "the same" record.

## First steps when a record is available

First hold zip-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command constant, then replace only the current revision. ARCA-003 documents exactly this type of comparison: do not change the entry point, command, and revision at the same time. The goal of the comparison isn't to turn the result green, but to find the first point where it changes.

If it still stalls after replacing the revision, don't immediately blame the revision; you still need to check whether the current entry point is the same one. Conversely, if the behavior changes, that only shows that this replacement is worth retaining; it cannot by itself prove that the exit action or permissions changed.

The scope of further work within the project includes records left by zip-quality-signal, the generation command, and the resources used for that run. If a needed record is inaccessible due to permissions, don't have the person taking over switch to guessing: send the current entry point and the saved evidence to the permissions owner. The permissions owner handles only access and return issues; whether it falls under zip-quality-signal is still determined by the existing records.

## Branch: resources not yet returned

When the current revision is on loan, first record the borrower, start time, and return window on the original card; ARCA-008 retained this logging requirement. Until the window closes, don't count waiting for resources as failure recovery. Revisit the current entry point only after the window closes, and distinguish in the notes whether you're seeing an old cache or an old task.

This page does not recast waiting for resources as an exit action. An exit action must be traceable to its original request; if all that's left of the page is a screenshot, obtain the original request first. A screenshot can show what was seen at the time, but it cannot replace the record it was supposed to link to.

## Single-environment behavior

When the source code and command are unchanged and only one environment fails, rerun in another environment as described in ARCA-013 and record the current revision. If it doesn't reproduce in the second environment, that doesn't mean the first one has recovered; it only limits the next step to differences between the environments or differences in the current entry point. If it still reproduces in the second environment, don't bypass the records and jump straight to declaring a shared cause.

In one case in ARCA-013, only a screenshot remained, and the original request corresponding to the exit entry point had not been attached. The stopping point for cases like this is therefore clear: retain the observations the screenshot supports, and don't continue explaining the exit action if you can't obtain the original request.

## What to include in the handoff

When handing off for work within the zip-quality-signal project, include the current entry point, the location of the original record, the current revision, and the single-variable comparisons already performed. When handing off to the permissions owner, include the inaccessible object and the evidence you have; do not include a root-cause conclusion. If exit-action handling is needed, include the original request; if it is missing, mark that item as not obtained.

The handoff entry point is still `docs/adj-zip/runbooks/zip-quality-signal-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`. On this page, stop at the first point where a record is missing, permissions are lacking, or the original request is needed.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Stall Troubleshooting Tree

Start by checking what is still available at the current entry point. When zip-quality-signal is stuck, a page that no longer changes, records that do not match, and an entry point that remains unchanged after the resource window has ended may all be called "stuck"; they are not the same thing. When on call, first place the observed behavior in the tree below, then decide whether to continue within the project, perform an exit action, or hand it over to the permissions owner. Each section of the tree only requires obtaining the records needed for the next section; stop if they cannot be obtained.

```text
Does the current entry point have original records that can be traced back to that run?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only screenshots remain
│  │  └─ Keep the screenshots; obtain the original request. Stop if the original request has not been found.
│  └─ No screenshots either
│     └─ Record the current entry point and missing items; do not determine the root cause.
└─ Yes
   ├─ The records still point to zip-quality-signal
   │  ├─ The current entry point, command, and current revision can be confirmed
   │  │  └─ Run one comparison that replaces only the current revision
   │  └─ Any one of these cannot be confirmed
   │     └─ Obtain that item; do not substitute a rerun for the original state
   ├─ The records point to an exit action
   │  └─ Find the original request corresponding to the action; if it cannot be found, stop at the exit entry point
   └─ Required records are not visible because of permissions
      └─ Hand over to the permissions owner, including the current entry point and preserved state
```

Original records here means records that connect the current entry point to that run, not summaries compiled later. Seeing a green state after a failure shows that there was a green state later; it does not show that the earliest failure has been explained. First save the original input, current revision, first result displayed, and command used to generate it; if any item cannot be found, explicitly identify the missing item. Do not backfill the original state with results from another environment, another record, or a page updated later.

## Start from the Entry Point, Not from Impressions

If the current entry point still opens, first confirm which run it displays. Old values on the page may come from an old cache or an old task; do not conflate these two cases before records are available. ARCA-021 specifically preserves the case where "the current entry point still shows old values after the window ends": first record the window's end time, then confirm whether the entry point retains an old cache or an old task. The end of the window is only the time to check again, not evidence that resources have been returned or that the task has exited.

If the entry point directly provides records for zip-quality-signal, keep the investigation within the project for now. Run a comparison only when the current entry point, command, and current revision all match up. The comparison in ARCA-003 has a very narrow scope: keep zip-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and replace only the current revision. The purpose is to find the first point of change, not to stop once a green result is found.

During the comparison, keep separate records for the original run and the run after replacing the revision. If it is still stuck after the replacement, that alone does not justify attributing the problem to the revision; check whether both runs still started from the same current entry point. If the behavior changes, do not directly describe the change as an exit action or a permissions change either. The comparison only establishes that the current revision is the condition that changed; the other conditions still need to be confirmed by records.

Without original records, a rerun is not a remedy either. Results from a rerun belong to a new state, even if the command looks identical. At this point, record only the current entry point, any screenshots still available, and the missing objects; the person taking over should first find the original request or collect the missing data, rather than continue adding interpretations to the screenshots.

## An Exit Entry Point with Only Screenshots

A common wrong turn in the exit-action branch is to see a screenshot and treat it as evidence of the exit action. A screenshot can only show that someone saw a particular page or result at that time; it cannot replace the original request corresponding to the exit action. ARCA-013 previously had this gap: only screenshots remained, and the original request corresponding to the exit entry point had not been attached.

When you encounter this state, follow this order:

1. Save what the screenshot shows about the page, without cropping it to support a conclusion.
2. Find the original request corresponding to the exit action.
3. Once the original request is found, link the current entry point to that request.
4. If the original request cannot be found, stop at the exit entry point; do not reclassify the exit action as an internal failure of zip-quality-signal, or as a permissions issue.

Stopping does not mean the screenshot is useless. It can still help the next person identify the earliest page seen, but it cannot independently establish who triggered the action, when it was triggered, or whether it has completed. If the exit action needs further handling, the handoff should include the current entry point, screenshot location, and whether the original request has been obtained; if it has not, explicitly write "not obtained".

## Resource Windows and the Current revision

While resources are still within the borrowing period, do not treat waiting for resources as recovery from a failure, or describe waiting for resources as an exit that has already completed. ARCA-008 requires writing the borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision back to the original card. This allows later checks to see the window itself, rather than just an entry point that has stopped progressing.

Window not yet ended: preserve the state and wait until the window ends before checking the current entry point again. Do not use this as a reason to start a new batch of reruns, or as grounds to conclude that the old values at the current entry point come from a cache.

Window ended: record the end time, then confirm whether the current entry point shows an old cache or an old task. If the records indicate an old cache, continue looking for records related to that cache; if they indicate an old task, continue looking for that task's run records. If there are no records for either, return to the "original records missing" node. The resource return record does not replace this determination.

A single-variable comparison of the current revision can be performed when all records are available, but it must not be combined with the resource-window assessment in one operation. First record the borrower, start time, and return window, then keep zip-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command fixed. If the revision and resource state change at the same time, even a green page will not tell you which change affected the behavior.

## Stopping Points for a Failure in Only One Environment

When the source code and command are unchanged and only one environment fails, follow the procedure in ARCA-013 to rerun in another environment, and record the current revision. Results from the second environment are only used to determine whether environment differences remain, not to overwrite the original records from the first environment.

- Not reproduced in the other environment: keep each environment's results and the current revision. Differences in the first environment or the current entry point may still be responsible, so do not declare recovery.
- Reproduced in the other environment as well: preserve this finding and return to the records for zip-quality-signal; do not move directly to shared handling just because both environments failed.
- Cannot rerun in the second environment: record why the rerun cannot be performed. Do not write "not reproduced" when it was "not rerun".

This branch handles failures in only one environment, not exit actions. If, before the rerun, you discover that the current entry point actually points to an exit entry point, stop the environment comparison and first find the corresponding original request. If the records needed for the rerun are not visible, follow the permissions branch first as well.

## Two Records Do Not Match

When the two sides' records for zip · Quality Signal Board do not match, do not overwrite one with the newer page from the other. The procedure in ARCA-026 is to compare the commands and times used to generate the two records, and stop at the first divergence. Everything before the first divergence can be preserved as a common state; from the first divergence onward, do not merge the two records into one continuous process.

```text
Were the two records generated with the same command?
├─ No: stop at the command difference
└─ Yes
   ├─ Can the generation times be aligned?
   │  ├─ No: stop at the time difference
   │  └─ Yes: continue confirming the current entry point each record points to
   └─ Missing times: obtain the times; do not decide which record is authoritative
```

"Stop at the first divergence" does not mean identifying the party ultimately responsible. It means the handoff must allow the next maintainer to continue from the same difference, rather than from two summaries that overwrite each other. If the commands differ, hand over to the side maintaining the generation command; if the commands are identical but one record is not visible because of permissions, hand over to the permissions owner; if both records open but the entry point has changed to an exit action, switch to obtaining the original request.

## Scope of the Permissions Owner

The permissions owner handles cases where "required records or objects are inaccessible". Include just three things in the handoff: the current entry point, original records or screenshots already confirmed, and the specific inaccessible object. Do not also hand over an unconfirmed revision, environment difference, or exit action as the root cause.

Once permissions are restored, the person taking over resumes from the nearest confirmed node in the original tree. For example, if the original records have been found and only another generated record is not visible, return to "Two Records Do Not Match"; if the original request for the exit action is not visible, return to "An Exit Entry Point with Only Screenshots". Resolving the permissions issue does not automatically close the incident for zip-quality-signal.

Handling within the project covers the parts that existing records explicitly link to zip-quality-signal, including the current entry point, generation command, current revision, resource borrowing records, and environment rerun records. Before going beyond these objects to explain behavior in other projects, confirm the interface records; if they cannot be confirmed, do not broaden the conclusions further.

## Handoff Package and Completion Conditions

When handing over within the zip-quality-signal project, include the current entry point, original record location, current revision, command, and any completed single-variable comparisons or environment reruns. When handing over to the exit-action entry point, include the status of the original request; if screenshots exist but the original request is missing, this gap must be preserved. When handing over to the permissions owner, include the inaccessible object and preserved state.

There are only three situations in which the current section of troubleshooting can end: the records clearly place the issue within zip-quality-signal, the exit action has an original request that can be matched to it, or the permissions owner has received the handoff for the inaccessible object. All other states remain at their stopping points in the tree. For the related single-variable comparison, see ARCA-003; for resource-window records, see ARCA-008; for reruns of single-environment failures, see ARCA-013; for old values after the window, see ARCA-021; for the first divergence between two records, see ARCA-026.

The handoff entry point is `docs/adj-zip/runbooks/zip-quality-signal-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`.

versions.body:
# Archive Library On-Call Rotation Decision Record

This record was originally intended only to document a disagreement during handoff: the existing streaming entry point was already in use, and some people also wanted to change the window during the rotation. If both were changed at the same time, it would be hard to tell whether subsequent differences came from the entry point or from the window changing the observation conditions. The initial draft therefore said "retain the entry point, leave the window unchanged for now". When this wording was revisited later, it seemed overly terse, as though it simply favored making no changes; the additional materials reviewed showed that what was actually decided at the time was a narrowly scoped arrangement.

This round approved continuing to use the current streaming entry point as an unchanged starting point for examining the archive lifecycle. Window adjustments were deferred, and were not included among the actions approved for this round. Here, "deferred" does not mean that there is a problem with the window itself, nor does it mean that the window may not be adjusted in the future; it only means that the materials available at the time did not distinguish window changes from differences at the entry point, stream, and file.

The assessment diagram retained from the rotation discussion is shown below. It is neither an execution sequence nor a module ownership diagram; both boundaries need to see the same input, and if either side is missing, the observations cannot be recorded as a complete lifecycle assessment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Current streaming entry point] --> B[Same input]
    B --> C[stream boundary]
    B --> D[file boundary]
    C --> E[Assessment for this round]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Retain the first output]
    E --> G[Window adjustments deferred]
```

One reminder in the meeting materials was never recast as formal terminology, but is still worth preserving alongside the decision:

> Read the frozen Ruby interfaces and their callers before assigning ownership; an archive lifecycle decision is trusted only when the same input is observable at both stream and file boundaries.

The first thing this statement changed was not code location, but how issues were assigned to the right place during the rotation. At the time, the review began with `lib/zip/file.rb` and several call names. This path could help locate the file side, but it did not imply that the file bore full responsibility for the archive lifecycle. At one point, the initial draft made "found via the file entry point" sound close to "should be handled by the file entry point", and this inference was removed after review. An interface's callers may still determine how input reaches a boundary; looking at only one file makes it easy to mistake the starting point of a search for long-term ownership.

Likewise, stream should not be treated as a word that can provide an answer on its own. The streaming entry point discussed here is the entry point retained at the time, not all internal processing performed in a stream-based manner. The file boundary is also only one side that needs to be examined alongside the other, and does not equate to `lib/zip/file.rb` being the sole point of responsibility. What the rotation needed was not a permanent map of the two, but confirmation, before deciding how to handle the issue, that both sides were seeing the same input.

Three approaches were compared in some detail at the time, and preserving them here is more useful than simply recording "the window was not changed":

| Approach | Action this round | Reason at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current streaming entry point | Approved | The entry point could serve as a starting point for inspection unaffected by window changes |
| Adjust the window during handoff | Deferred | It was not possible to tell whether differences observed after the adjustment should be attributed to the window, stream, or file |
| Use the file entry point to directly assign responsibility for handling | Not adopted | Filenames and call names only provided search clues, and the interfaces and their callers had not yet been bypassed |
| Keep the last output after rerunning | Not adopted | It would overwrite the state that already existed at the time of the first failure |

The third item was easy to misread at the time as "there is no ownership". That was not what it meant. The rotation did not approve a fixed mapping from entry points to people or modules, because the review conducted so far did not provide enough support for it; but it did not give up on addressing the issue as a result. The action already agreed on was to first read the frozen Ruby interfaces and their callers, then make an assessment based on the same input on both the stream and file sides. Directly naming `lib/zip/file.rb` as the permanent handoff point would cause later readers to skip this step and repeat the initial draft's misreading.

How reruns after failures are handled is another indispensable part of this decision. The requirement is to retain the first output and not overwrite the original state. The intent is not to accumulate a batch of copies in the same format, but to retain the output left by the first failure. If a rerun overwrites it directly, later reviewers will only have the later state: they will not know whether the failure was already present at the outset, will not know whether the rerun changed the conditions, and will be unable to confirm whether the two observations corresponded to the same input.

This is directly related to deferring window adjustments. A window change could make the conditions during a rerun differ from those of the first failure; if the original output were also overwritten, the record would lose both the state before comparison and the basis for comparison. As a result, the approach of "adjusting the window first, then taking the rerun result as authoritative" was not included in this round. It would not necessarily cause an error, but it did not leave enough information to determine whether it could still bring the same input to both boundaries for cross-checking.

The initial draft's old wording about reruns is preserved below to help explain why it was later narrowed:

> As long as an output is left when the rerun finishes, it is sufficient for subsequent assessment.

That statement subsequently ceased to apply. The last output can show what happened at the end of the rerun, but cannot substitute for the state of the first failure. The revised approach applies only to reruns after a failure: leave the first output in place, examine the rerun results separately, and do not use the latter to erase the former. This is not a long-term retention approach covering all run results.

Another wording change removed "check stream first, then file" as the description of the inspection. This order had once made rotation handoffs easier, but it misrepresented the main point. The order alone cannot establish the relationship between the two sides; what must be confirmed is that both sides receive the same input. If the stream assessment comes from one set of materials and the impression of file comes from another, the two checks should not be combined into a single archive lifecycle assessment, even if both have been performed. During review, that sentence was changed to a parallel requirement covering both boundaries, and the decision to retain the entry point remained unchanged.

The window proposal was not left entirely undiscussed either. Those in favor of an adjustment wanted to use the handoff window as a new starting point for observation, to avoid continuing to add more handling around the existing entry point. The objections did not say that such an arrangement was unworkable, but pointed out that it would add another condition changing at the same time. If the entry point, window, and rerun method all changed together, it would be hard to return to the original state and explain the differences after a failure occurred. There was no explanation at the time of how to retain the first output after the window changed, nor of how stream and file could still be checked against the same input before and after the change, so it was not approved.

"Retain the entry point" has not been elevated here into a general rule for archive read/write paths. It was a choice made during the rotation: leave an existing observation point unchanged for now, so subsequent review can identify where differences came from. Extending this to say that all archive entry points should remain unchanged goes beyond the original discussion. Likewise, the deferral of window adjustments cannot be used to claim that window arrangements in other handoffs have already been rejected.

During review, someone also wanted to add a fixed responsibility table: stream on one side, file on the other, and the window handled by the handoff party. This suggestion did not become part of the decision. It would have made the record look more complete, but would have obscured what was actually missing at the time—how callers send input to the interfaces, and whether both sides really see the same input. Without these relationships, a responsibility table would merely present the guesses more neatly.

Retaining the first output also does not mean that every failure can already be reproduced. It only prevents reruns from overwriting what was seen first. The first output may still be insufficient to explain the failure, may lack observations at one of the boundaries, or later inspection may reveal that the inputs were not the same. These situations require returning to the interfaces and their callers for further review, and the window must not be moved first, nor may the next rerun be treated as a substitute for the first failure.

When reading this page later, the safer way to use it is as a record of choices within a single rotation: the existing streaming entry point was retained; window adjustments were not approved; reruns after failures must not overwrite the first output; ownership must not be determined solely from `lib/zip/file.rb` or call names. These points explain why changes were not introduced into the window at the time, but do not constitute a new archive lifecycle operations manual.

For the switchover handoff related to the dependency upgrade window, see DOC-44. That material addresses local arrangements at the handoff; the two records can serve as cross-references, but this should not be used to infer retrospectively that window adjustments had already been approved in this round.

One question remains undecided: if the same input yields observations on the stream and file sides that cannot be reconciled, the first step should be to return to the frozen interfaces and their callers to identify the differences, rather than eliminate the differences by adjusting the window or overwriting the first output. As to where such differences should ultimately be handled, no decision was made in this round.

# Cross-Platform Regression Entry Point Code Walkthrough

Start at `internal/archive-core/lib/zip/file.rb`. This time, we're not looking for every implementation that mentions streaming. We're looking for the first place in cross-platform regression that actually uses the result after the public entry point hands it off.

Follow just one hop first. Once the entry point is confirmed, note the object it calls directly, then check whether that object carries the same result into the regression path. Treat files that share a name, live in the same directory, or also handle streaming as signposts at this stage; those facts alone don't put them in the call chain.

```text
streaming public entry point
        |
        v
direct caller
        |
        v
consumer in cross-platform regression
```

# Tracing the Cross-Platform Regression Entry Point

This review still starts from `internal/archive-core/lib/zip/file.rb`. A file location can only lead us near the public entry point; it cannot replace the call relationship. What we need to narrow down here is a question easily skewed by directories and names: starting from streaming's public entry point, go through only one direct caller to find where the cross-platform regression first actually uses its result.

After the entry point, we are not trying to draw the entire regression chain. There may be comparisons, platform handling, or wrapper layers after the cross-platform regression; pulling those in early would make readers think they are all directly triggered by the current entry point. This page retains only the short stretch of relationships that can be followed continuously from the entry point.

## Start from the Entry Point

First confirm streaming's public entry point in the file, then see whom the entry point hands off to. Here, "who" is not a file guessed from a similar name, but a direct caller the entry point actually reaches. When reading this hop, focus not on collecting every potentially relevant location, but on distinguishing whether the caller received the result itself or only an object used to continue the search.

```text
streaming public entry point
        |
        v
one direct caller
        |
        v
first real consumer in the cross-platform regression
```

Confirm the second arrow in the diagram from the call relationship as well. If the direct caller only forwards the result, continue by checking where it hands the result off; if it changes the result before the handoff, first record that change on this hop, then determine whether the subsequent regression location is still consuming the same result. Stop when reaching the first real consumer; do not add assertions and platform branches after the consumer to this call graph.

## What to Leave at Each Hop

At the entry point, write only the call actually issued by the entry point and where the result goes. Do not list adjacent files returned by the search in this slot; that would disguise the scope of the search as a confirmed adjacency relationship.

At the direct caller, distinguish between two cases. It may simply pass the entry point's result onward, or it may process that result before handing it to the regression side. For the former, recording the handoff direction is enough; for the latter, state explicitly that the change occurred at the direct-caller hop, rather than attributing the change to the regression consumer.

At the consumer, confirm only the location of the "first use." By first, we mean the first actual use reached along the current entry point, not the file where the same term appears earliest in the directory, nor the assertion location later in the regression chain that is easier to understand. If the same object can be seen at both locations, retain the one closer to the entry point and with a call edge.

A short note may be left beside each segment: whether this is a call fact, a locator trail, or a handoff that still needs clarification. This prevents the original search clues from being misread during a later review as an already confirmed path determination. The record does not need to expand into an object inventory; one entry point, one direct call, and one consumer location are enough to support this review.

## `byte`, `owner`, and digest

During the search, use `streaming` to land at the entry point first, then use `byte` and `owner` to cross-check nearby handoffs. `byte` is a term that helps find traces of result processing here; a single hit does not make it evidence of the consumer. `owner` likewise only helps identify a handoff location that needs further inquiry; it is not a fixed node name in the current path.

`unchanged-byte digest` is locator material intentionally retained for this review. During the trace, note which side it appears on: the public entry point, the direct caller, or the first consumer. If the digest is on the consumer side, it can be retained together with that consumer's actual use; if it appears only in an adjacent file, first return to the segment between the entry point and the direct caller to check whether a direct pass-through exists.

The position of the digest cannot replace a call edge. Even if a file leaves behind a unchanged-byte digest, it may only be adjacent to the current flow; conversely, a confirmed direct caller may not be the location where the digest was left. Writing these two judgments separately avoids mistaking "processed byte" for "already entered the cross-platform regression."

## Do Not Extend the Chain by Name

Same-named files, files in the same directory, and implementations that also mention streaming can all serve as waypoints for returning to the search, but they do not enter the main path unless a call edge connecting to them is visible from the current node. Especially near the entry point, name similarity can easily cause someone to skip the intermediate handoff and directly call a seemingly related file the consumer.

During actual reading, if a candidate file has no relationship from the current entry point to it, mark it as a waypoint beside the path and return to the previous hop; do not fill in its result source or include it in the diagram. This leaves a shorter path, but readers can tell which nodes have been confirmed and which are merely stopping points for the next search.

If it is unclear where the direct caller's result goes, do not infer backward from another same-named implementation. First retain the segment from the entry point to the direct caller, and leave the unclear handoff at the end. The value of the trace is preserving direction, not compressing all possible branches into an apparently complete chain.

## The First Version and This Review

The initial version only established the direction: "search from streaming to find the public entry point, then follow one layer." At the time, `byte` and `owner` were recorded as possible search terms, and `unchanged-byte digest` was also merely a location to mark along the way. That record did not clearly distinguish same-named files from real consumers, nor did it specify which hop the result handoff should stop at.

What this review adds is this distinction: after the public entry point, follow only one direct caller until the first real consumer in the cross-platform regression. It is not an archive of all cross-platform regression implementations, nor an explanation of the subsequent comparison logic. The earlier wording that treated name-similar locations as possible consumers is now retained only for waypoint use.

The review still did not produce more detailed function names, parameter shapes, or platform-branch material, so these were not written into the path. Readers who want to continue tracing the processing after the consumer should start a separate trace from the confirmed consumer, rather than extending this page's three-segment path into the entire regression flow.

## Stop at the Handoff Boundary

When any of the following occurs, the current trace ends at the last node that can be confirmed: only a same-named file was found and there is no call edge; the result can be seen being handed off, but it cannot be confirmed who uses it first; or the meaning of the handoff requires an explanation from another owner. At that point, leave the entry point, the direct caller, the location of the last locatable `unchanged-byte digest`, and the unconfirmed handoff.

Do not guess the consumer's name to make the graph close, and do not write an adjacent implementation as the caller. When the path does not close, a short path is still more useful than an incorrect long path. The part requiring further confirmation should remain at the final hop, rather than being filled back into the entry-point description.

# Maintenance Docs Cleanup Discrepancy Postmortem

During the maintenance docs cleanup window, the results visible on the page did not match the original plan. When this was discovered, the discrepancy could not yet be attributed to a particular file, permission, or archive operation; all that was confirmed at the time was that the results were not displayed as expected. This record retains the old term "cleanup discrepancy." It describes the state observed at the time, not a confirmed cause.

This affected the assessment of whether cleanup was complete during the window. Content that should have been directly verifiable under the plan could only be viewed after access was temporarily reestablished. As a result, on-call staff could not declare cleanup complete based solely on the page state, nor assume that the issue had been fully explained just because the content later became visible again.

## Timeline

- After cleanup started in the window, the visible results differed from the original plan.
- On initial discovery, a minimal archive fixture was retained; the captured state was not expanded into a full archive sample.
- Temporary recovery followed, allowing inspection to continue during the window.
- Before the release window ended, a control was added requiring the temporary directories and access permissions to be returned.
- When this record was closed out, the specific cause of the discrepancy was still unknown.

At the time, the minimal archive fixture was retained only to preserve the minimal object on which this discrepancy depended. It did not cover all maintenance docs, nor was it used to prove that archive contents, directory presentation, and access state were necessarily related in the same way. Anyone revisiting this fixture later should first confirm that they are examining the visible results from the window, rather than mistaking it for a complete recovery sample.

The temporary recovery addressed the immediate inability to continue inspecting. The old record described this step in terms close to "the window was restored." Looking back, that wording was too broad: returning the temporary directories and access permissions only showed that the temporary arrangements were not kept in use past the release window. It did not establish the root cause of the discrepancy or prove that the original plan had no omissions.

The missed control in this incident was at closeout, not at initial discovery. Temporary directories and access permissions retained during cleanup to verify the results must be returned before the release window ends. This requirement concerns the state left by this temporary recovery; it cannot be used to conclude that every maintenance cleanup requires the same recovery steps.

Only one point remains unconfirmed: why the original plan and the final visible results did not match. The available material is insufficient to determine whether the cleanup process, access conditions, or the display path caused the discrepancy. This unknown is retained so that later references to this record do not treat the temporary recovery as a conclusion about the cause.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Result Discrepancies in the Dependency Upgrade Window

The ticket says the dependency upgrade window is complete, but verification doesn't line up. Don't treat the completion status as the result.

```text
Results cannot be verified
├─ Can you identify the metadata call entry point?
│  ├─ No: note that the entry point still needs to be identified; stop.
│  └─ Yes: record the version associated with that entry point.
└─ Can the version be tied to this upgrade window?
   ├─ No: keep the "complete" flag; draw no conclusion; stop.
   └─ Yes: compare the unchanged-byte digest for the same input.
       ├─ Match: look for the discrepancy in the verification path first.
       └─ Mismatch: keep both outputs and their versions; ask the entry-point side for the missing information.
```

Hand back the temporary directories and access permissions before the release window ends.

Post-meeting note: the input for that verification was unchanged, but the metadata call entry point and version weren't recorded together. Neither the ticket's "completed" status nor the majority result from multiple reruns can be used to make a judgment here.

```text
Results cannot be verified
├─ Can you identify the metadata call entry point?
│  ├─ No: note the missing entry-point location; stop here.
│  └─ Yes: continue by finding the version in use when this entry point produced metadata.
├─ Does this version belong to this dependency upgrade window?
│  ├─ No: keep the ticket's completion status only as a record; do not compare digests; stop.
│  └─ Yes: obtain the unchanged-byte digest using the same input.
│      ├─ Match: check the display or verification path first; include the entry point and version.
│      └─ Mismatch: keep both outputs and their versions; ask the entry-point side to fill in how they were produced; stop.
```

The actual verification only got as far as "the same input": the entry point and version were still scattered across different records. The digest mismatch was therefore not recorded as a post-upgrade behavior change, and further reruns are not used to decide the issue. The tree stops at any point that requires new evidence.
